I had been in Wuhan for more than a month. Apart from going downtown for the IELTS exam or to deal with a few personal matters, I had not really taken the time to see the city simply as a tourist. Then, this week, I came across an interesting Wuhan-based creator. They used characters from my favorite anime, Bocchi the Rock! , to visit restaurants all over Wuhan, and the videos were edited in a very entertaining way I kept watching one more episode . The food was also exactly the kind I like. Since I had been worrying about having nowhere to go, I decided to follow the creator's route for a day. Route: The rest of this diary follows that route through the day. The Creator's Recommendation! Or perhaps I should say, the recommended creator, hehe ¬◡¬ ✧ This creator posts videos on Bilibili. I happened to scroll onto this one and discovered that Wuhan had a Michelin restaurant that was this affordable! Since I had just arrived in Wuhan and did not know where to begin exploring, I made up my mind to visit it on the weekend. Macau Chan Kwong Kee Roast Meat Restaurant This was the restaurant mentioned in the creator's video. I set out early, spent more than an hour on the metro, and arrived at the storefront. The restaurant is in central Wuhan, less than 200 meters along the road from the northwest gate of Zhongshan Park. There is no commercial street around it and no flashy sign—only a simple, plain storefront. A school stands across the road, so the restaurant feels like the small noodle shops often found outside primary schools: quietly existing there and tending to its modest business. Next came the ordering. I did not follow the creator's recommendations; treating it as my first visit, I ordered a few things I personally like: Chilled tofu pudding, double-combo rice, char siu pastry, pineapple ice, and lau nai wah—a Hong Kong-style French toast dessert. Neither the tofu pudding nor the pineapple ice was particularly surprising, but both were solid and satisfying. The tofu pudding had absolutely no beany smell. It carried a faint soybean fragrance, was smooth and tender, and came with osmanthus honey that was not cloying or harsh on the throat. It was cold, refreshing, and wonderfully thirst-quenching. As a soda, the pineapple ice was barely sweet; nearly all the sweetness came from the melted ice cream and pineapple. Its only flaw was that there was not enough of it to drink with abandon. The double-combo rice and char siu pastry were what really surprised me. The moment these two dishes entered my mouth, the only word that came to mind was: satisfaction. First, the double-combo rice. The fatty char siu was pleasantly springy, with a rich sauce aroma. A little honey drizzled over it added another layer of flavor. The fat was soft and bouncy rather than greasy enough to coat the mouth unpleasantly. The roast duck had skin as thin as paper; eaten together with the sauce beneath it, it perfectly compensated for the slightly dry texture of the duck meat itself. It was not flawless, though. As the photos show, the plate was covered with a glossy layer of oil mixed with the honey drizzle. By the second half of the meal, it became somewhat rich and difficult for someone like me—who had been eating relatively lightly recently—to digest. Now, the honey-glazed char siu pastry. As soon as it arrived, it gave off the buttery, flaky aroma of a freshly baked pastry. Once I bit in, that fragrance filled my nose. Unlike at some restaurants, the honey glaze did not contain undissolved sugar crystals that scraped against the teeth. Perhaps it was because the pastry had just been baked, or perhaps the honey water had been mixed to exactly the right concentration so that it would not crystallize. The meat filling had been cut into tiny pieces. Yet once I pressed it with my tongue, it did not feel like a collection of separate chunks. I suspect they used fatty meat from a cut with little connective tissue, so it did not interfere with the texture. It was deeply satisfying. I did not really enjoy the lau nai wah. To me, it was pure sugar-and-fat. After the double-combo rice and char siu pastry, I needed something lighter to cleanse my palate, and ordering it after the meal was a mistake that got in the way of enjoying it. I will keep that in mind next time. As the first Michelin restaurant of my life, it left me very satisfied. At around ¥100 per person, it was also affordable. I would like to return one day and try the creator's recommendations. Zhongshan Park After lunch I was incredibly full. My reservation at the provincial museum was not until 3 p.m., so there was still plenty of time. I decided to walk around the nearby Zhongshan Park. The trees in the park were extremely thick and tall, suggesting that Zhongshan Park had existed here for a very long time. I was surprised to find a fairly substantial amusement park as well: a small roller coaster, a pirate ship, and several other medium-sized rides, all built in 2023. The classic boating attraction was still there too. It was a case of “old trees growing new branches”—the park retained the steadiness of its history while also feeling lively and fresh. After a simple walk through Zhongshan Park to digest lunch, I set off for the Hubei Provincial Museum to finally meet the Sword of Goujian, King of Yue, and the Marquis Yi of Zeng's bronze bells—two treasures I had been looking forward to seeing. Hubei Provincial Museum My reservation was for 3 p.m., but I arrived at 2:20. To give every visitor the best possible experience, the museum only allows entry up to 20 minutes before the reserved time be sure to note this! . As soon as I entered, I hurried toward the South Hall, where the Sword of Goujian is displayed. Even after entering the museum, getting a glimpse of the real sword required a long wait. Only then could I look at it for a few seconds among the crowd surrounding the display case. The sword is 55.7 centimeters long; the blade is 4.6 centimeters wide; the hilt is 8.4 centimeters long; and it weighs 875 grams. Both sides of the blade bear dark diamond-shaped patterns. The front of the guard is set with blue glaze, while the back has a turquoise pattern. The pommel is a circular ring containing 11 concentric circles. The entire blade was treated with sulfurization, greatly improving its corrosion resistance and toughness. This shows that ancient Chinese metallurgists had reached a remarkably high level of skill in metal smelting and surface treatment. When unearthed, the sword still shone coldly and was extraordinarily sharp. It reflects the advanced sword-making technology of ancient China and is a rare treasure among ancient weapons. —Wikipedia The whole sword was only about as long as a forearm—much smaller than I had imagined. It looked a little like an ancient person's collectible figure although according to the information, it was still a practical weapon . Seeing the real object was different from seeing it on television. We could not make out the details, but the museum had a complete exhibition and introduction devoted to the sword, and I still learned a great deal. Next, I headed for the second national treasure: the bronze bells of Marquis Yi of Zeng. The set of bells belonging to Marquis Yi of Zeng is enormous and completely intact. The bell frame is tall, formed from two perpendicular wooden structures of different lengths. The longer side lies to the west of the tomb and is 7.48 meters long and 2.65 meters high; the side toward the south is 3.35 meters long and 2.73 meters high. Seven painted wooden beams run through the frame, reinforced at both ends with bronze fittings decorated with coiled dragons. Six cast-bronze warriors wearing swords and eight columns support the entire set of bells, forming upper, middle, and lower tiers. The frame and its hooks number 246 in total. The bronze figures wear long robes, belts around their waists, and solemn expressions. —Wikipedia The hall containing the bells was much larger. Its display panels explained the details of Marquis Yi, the excavation, and the other instruments used alongside the bells. There were also bronze objects of all sizes around them. Their shapes and details were beyond anything I had imagined. Even with today's technology and methods, I am not sure they could be perfectly reproduced. There were many more national treasures, but here I will simply record a few that impressed me most. Huahua Pizza After the museum, I went to another restaurant recommended by the creator mentioned at the beginning: Huahua Pizza. The decor was simple and attractive, bright and fresh, and the street outside was very clean. Since lunch had left me extremely full, I ordered an eight-inch Margherita pizza ¥20 and a serving of fried chicken, the restaurant's top seller. The Margherita pizza arrived first. The price was fairly reasonable. A street cart I often visit in Xiamen sells a nine-inch pizza for the same ¥20, although this restaurant has a much nicer environment. Overall, it tasted fine—it tasted like a Margherita pizza, and I am not sure what else a Margherita pizza is supposed to do... Let me mention a few disappointments. First, the basil had been baked until slightly bitter and had lost its fresh fragrance, and there was not much of it. I really like the aroma of basil, but I could barely taste it here. Second, although the pizza was made to order, the wheat aroma of the crust was not prominent enough and the crust was not chewy enough. That was a little disappointing. Next came the restaurant's best-selling boneless fried chicken, which the creator had recommended enthusiastically. Even with expectations that high, the plate still surprised me. The crust was not merely crisp; it was coated in enormous bread crumbs, and the crust alone could compete with packaged potato chips. The base seasoning of the meat was balanced: it did not overpower the chicken's own flavor, but you could still taste the care that had gone into seasoning it. More importantly, the chicken inside was full of juice. Dipped into the sauce provided, the entire portion was not greasy even when eaten by one person. If you want a satisfying meal on a small budget, this restaurant is genuinely worth visiting. Conclusion Following “氵皮ki酱” led me to two restaurants and showed me that Wuhan has not only a formidable history but also an incredibly rich food scene. My stomach was full, but my heart felt strangely empty—there were still so many recommended restaurants I had not had time to visit and so many sights I had not had time to see. But that is all right. This was only the beginning of one of my many weekends in Wuhan. My exam preparation continues, but whenever I have free time, I will keep exploring the city's different sides. After all, life is not only about the hardship immediately before us 11408 ; it also includes Wuhan's hidden restaurants and the next journey of discovery.

items.title: TCP Slow-Start Window Growth: A Three-Level Comparison of Textbooks, RFCs, and the Linux Kernel
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some technical wording may differ from the original; please refer to the cited RFCs and source code for authoritative details. While studying for my exam a few days ago, I came across this question: You can view it here: 2025 exam question The answer's explanation said: Since the current congestion window is smaller than the threshold, the connection is in the slow-start phase. For every ACK received, the congestion window increases by 1 MSS, so it grows from 2000 B to 3000 B. This small detail was different from my long-standing assumption that the congestion window doubles after every RTT. What was going on? As it turned out, I had simply failed to read the textbook carefully 🤪. TCP also uses cumulative acknowledgments, so would that not prevent the window from doubling? With this question in mind, I asked a very capable classmate. Their answer was: The sender grows according to the number of bytes acknowledged, not the number of ACKs. When one ACK acknowledges one MSS, you can also think of it as growing according to the ACK count. The exact implementation depends on the protocol design. Many networking questions describe an idealized situation. This introduced yet another explanation: growth according to acknowledged bytes? I became curious about how actually grows during TCP slow start, so I decided to investigate it myself. Starting with “Doubling Every RTT” Let us begin with the description most familiar from networking textbooks and exam questions. The initial congestion window is usually set to 1 MSS the latest RFCs allow more MSS . The slow-start algorithm says that for every acknowledgment of a new segment, increases by 1. In this way, after each transmission round—one round-trip time, or RTT— doubles, producing exponential growth as transmission rounds pass. To prevent from growing without limit, a slow-start threshold called is also set. When grows to , slow start stops and the congestion-avoidance algorithm takes over. It can be summarized like this: During slow start: for every ACK, . If every data segment in one RTT triggers its own ACK, roughly doubles by the end of that RTT. During congestion avoidance: growth slows to approximately 1 MSS per RTT. Assume that the threshold is 16. The example looks like this: Round Initial cwnd ACKs received during one RTT cwnd at the end of the RTT ----- ------------ ---------------------------- ------------------------------- 0 1 MSS 1 2 MSS 1 2 MSS 2 4 MSS 2 4 MSS 4 8 MSS 3 8 MSS 8 16 MSS The slow start algorithm is used when cwnd ssthresh. When cwnd and ssthresh are equal, the sender may use either slow start or congestion avoidance. During slow start, a TCP increments cwnd by at most SMSS bytes for each ACK received that cumulatively acknowledges new data. Slow start ends when cwnd exceeds ssthresh or, optionally, when it reaches it, as noted above or when congestion is observed. While traditionally TCP implementations have increased cwnd by precisely SMSS bytes upon receipt of an ACK covering new data, we RECOMMEND that TCP implementations increase cwnd, per: cwnd += min N, SMSS 2 where N is the number of previously unacknowledged bytes acknowledged in the incoming ACK. This adjustment is part of Appropriate Byte Counting RFC3465 and provides robustness against misbehaving receivers that may attempt to induce a sender to artificially inflate cwnd using a mechanism known as "ACK Division" SCWA99 . ACK Division consists of a receiver sending multiple ACKs for a single TCP data segment, each acknowledging only a portion of its data. A TCP that increments cwnd by SMSS for each such ACK will inappropriately inflate the amount of data injected into the network. The core meaning of Section 3.1 of RFC 5681 is: During slow start, for each ACK that cumulatively acknowledges new data, TCP increases by the number of acknowledged bytes, but by no more than the sender's MSS bytes. This can be broken down into three key phrases: : an ACK is the trigger. : the ACK must cumulatively acknowledge new data. : is the number of bytes newly acknowledged by the ACK, capped at the sender's MSS. Why Is It Designed This Way? The original text explains the reason as well: This adjustment is part of Appropriate Byte Counting ABC, RFC 3465 , which makes TCP more robust against misbehaving receivers. An abnormal receiver might use a mechanism called ACK Division to induce the sender to inflate . In ACK Division, the receiver sends multiple ACKs for one TCP data segment, with each ACK acknowledging only a portion of that segment. If a TCP implementation increases by SMSS for every such ACK, it will inappropriately increase the amount of data injected into the network. In short, RFC 5681 wants to prevent the receiver from tricking the sender into expanding its congestion window by “splitting ACKs.” Suppose the sender transmits one data segment of size . Normally, the receiver should acknowledge the segment with one ACK. During slow start, the sender then increases by 1 SMSS, which is fine. But if the receiver deliberately splits the acknowledgment into several small ACKs: If the sender still follows the rule “increase by 1 SMSS for every ACK,” the same data segment will trigger multiple window increases. Only one segment was successfully transmitted through the network, but the sender behaves as though it can inject a great deal more data. is therefore inflated abnormally. This is why RFC 5681 recommends: The meaning is: If an ACK acknowledges only a small amount of new data, increases only by that amount. If an ACK acknowledges a large amount of data, the increase for that ACK is still capped at . This preserves the normal slow-start behavior—one fully acknowledged MSS produces roughly one MSS of growth—while preventing ACK Division from maliciously inflating the window. However, this is only the rule described by RFC 5681 / RFC 3465 from a byte-counting perspective. When we later look at the Linux kernel implementation, we will see a different viewpoint: Linux does not directly increase the window according to the number of newly acknowledged bytes. It counts the number of “fully acknowledged segments.” That difference is the most interesting part of this article. Linux Kernel Implementation: Why Does It Look Different Again? The source is in the Linux kernel s ; search for . Here is the core function and the comment immediately before it: The comment contains a great deal of information. Here is a copy version so we can see it more clearly: Slow start is used when the congestion window is no greater than the slow-start threshold. Linux is based on RFC 2581 and handles stretch ACKs correctly. Linux does not strictly implement Appropriate Byte Counting ABC from RFC 3465. Instead, it uses another approach: a packet is counted as acknowledged only when it has been fully ACKed or SACKed. This defends against the ACK attacks described in the RFC. For a stretch ACK with degree N, Linux's slow start treats it as though N ordinary ACKs of degree 1 had arrived back to back. ABC, however, caps N at 2. When this growth would make cross , slow start stops at the threshold and returns the unused ACK count to congestion avoidance so that congestion avoidance can continue adjusting the window. Several terms need explanation first: : Selective Acknowledgment, which tells the sender which non-contiguous data blocks have already arrived. : the notation used in the kernel comment, meaning ACKed or SACKed. : an ACK that acknowledges multiple segments at once instead of only one. For example, a receiver using delayed acknowledgment may wait for two or more TCP segments before sending one ACK. : this stretch ACK acknowledges N complete segments at once. Is Not Measured in Bytes The most important detail is that in this Linux function does not mean “how many bytes were acknowledged.” It means “how many complete segments were acknowledged.” RFC 5681 / RFC 3465 tends to describe the rule in bytes: Here, is the number of bytes newly acknowledged by the ACK. But the implementation here is closer to: Here, is the number of newly acknowledged complete segments. Linux itself maintains in segment units, so does not add a byte count directly to the window; it adds the number of complete segments acknowledged. This explains why the kernel code looks different from the RFC formula: RFC discussions often describe growth in bytes. Linux's here is the number of fully acknowledged data segments. Therefore, means that the window grows by the number of complete segments. Under ideal conditions, this is equivalent to the textbook rule “for every ACK, .” If an ACK acknowledges exactly one complete MSS, then and the window increases by one segment. Why Does This Also Prevent ACK Division? Linux's defense is different from the RFC's. It does not treat a fraction of a segment as one effective “complete-segment acknowledgment.” Only when a packet is fully acknowledged does it count toward . Therefore, even if a malicious receiver splits one segment into multiple small ACKs, cannot become multiple complete segments. That is what the comment means when it says: Linux does not strictly implement ABC, but does something “better.” “Better” here can be understood as defending against ACK Division at the granularity of complete-segment acknowledgments rather than at byte granularity. This can provide higher throughput, avoids floating-point and byte-level calculations, and transitions more smoothly into congestion avoidance. The code walkthrough below will explain that transition line by line. Linux Is More Aggressive with Stretch ACKs Now consider a stretch ACK. Suppose one ACK acknowledges three complete segments at once. Linux treats it as though three ordinary ACKs arrived consecutively. RFC 3465's ABC, by contrast, limits a single increase during slow start; its experimental recommendation says that should not exceed . Therefore, under a stretch ACK, Linux is somewhat more aggressive than ABC. This also explains the comment: Linux treats a stretch ACK that acknowledges N segments as N ordinary ACKs arriving back to back, while ABC limits that number to 2. The Code in Detail: Reading Line by Line Let us return to the function: First, several variables: : the control block for the current TCP connection, containing the connection's congestion-control state. : the current sender congestion window, measured in complete segments. : the slow-start threshold. Slow start grows only until approximately this threshold, after which congestion avoidance takes over. : the hard upper limit for the congestion window, preventing from exceeding the maximum allowed by the system. : the number of complete segments newly acknowledged by this ACK. The first line: calculates how far the window can grow during slow start: In other words, during slow start the window really does increase according to , but it cannot grow beyond . The second line: calculates how much of this ACK's acknowledgment count has already been consumed by slow start. is the amount by which slow start actually increased the window this time. Subtracting that amount from leaves the acknowledgment count that slow start did not use. What Happens When Is Reached? Consider this example: Without the threshold, the window could grow from 8 to 13. But slow start can only grow as far as : So slow start consumes only 2 of the 5 acknowledged segments: The third line: actually updates in the TCP control block. The value is also clamped against , ensuring that the window does not exceed the system's configured upper limit. The last line: returns the part of that slow start did not consume. If slow start has not reached , the function usually returns 0, meaning that the entire acknowledgment count was used to grow the slow-start window. If this ACK crosses the slow-start threshold, the function returns the remaining so that the congestion-avoidance logic can use it. While studying for my exam a few days ago, I came across this question:

You can view it here: 2025 exam question

The answer's explanation said:

Since the current congestion window is smaller than the threshold, the connection is in the slow-start phase. For every ACK received, the congestion window increases by 1 MSS, so it grows from 2000 B to 3000 B.

This small detail was different from my long-standing assumption that the congestion window doubles after every RTT. What was going on? (As it turned out, I had simply failed to read the textbook carefully 🤪.) TCP also uses cumulative acknowledgments, so would that not prevent the window from doubling?

With this question in mind, I asked a very capable classmate. Their answer was:

The sender grows cwnd according to the number of bytes acknowledged, not the number of ACKs. (When one ACK acknowledges one MSS, you can also think of it as growing cwnd according to the ACK count.) The exact implementation depends on the protocol design. Many networking questions describe an idealized situation.

This introduced yet another explanation: growth according to acknowledged bytes? I became curious about how cwnd actually grows during TCP slow start, so I decided to investigate it myself.

Starting with “Doubling Every RTT”

Let us begin with the description most familiar from networking textbooks and exam questions.

The initial congestion window cwnd is usually set to 1 MSS (the latest RFCs allow more MSS). The slow-start algorithm says that for every acknowledgment of a new segment, cwnd increases by 1. In this way, after each transmission round—one round-trip time, or RTT—cwnd doubles, producing exponential growth as transmission rounds pass. To prevent cwnd from growing without limit, a slow-start threshold called ssthresh is also set. When cwnd grows to ssthresh, slow start stops and the congestion-avoidance algorithm takes over.

It can be summarized like this:

  • During slow start: for every ACK, cwnd += 1 MSS.
  • If every data segment in one RTT triggers its own ACK, cwnd roughly doubles by the end of that RTT.
  • During congestion avoidance: growth slows to approximately 1 MSS per RTT.

Assume that the threshold is 16. The example looks like this:

Round Initial cwnd ACKs received during one RTT cwnd at the end of the RTT
0 1 MSS 1 2 MSS
1 2 MSS 2 4 MSS
2 4 MSS 4 8 MSS
3 8 MSS 8 16 MSS <-(threshold reached)
4 16 MSS 16 17 MSS <-(congestion avoidance)

So cwnd grows exponentially with each RTT. Even though modern TCP uses cumulative acknowledgments, its growth trend is still approximately exponential.

RFC 5681: How the Standard Defines Slow Start

You can find the original text here.

The slow start algorithm is used when cwnd < ssthresh, while the congestion avoidance algorithm is used when cwnd > ssthresh. When cwnd and ssthresh are equal, the sender may use either slow start or congestion avoidance.

During slow start, a TCP increments cwnd by at most SMSS bytes for each ACK received that cumulatively acknowledges new data. Slow start ends when cwnd exceeds ssthresh (or, optionally, when it reaches it, as noted above) or when congestion is observed. While traditionally TCP implementations have increased cwnd by precisely SMSS bytes upon receipt of an ACK covering new data, we RECOMMEND that TCP implementations increase cwnd, per:

cwnd += min (N, SMSS) (2)

where N is the number of previously unacknowledged bytes acknowledged in the incoming ACK. This adjustment is part of Appropriate Byte Counting [RFC3465] and provides robustness against misbehaving receivers that may attempt to induce a sender to artificially inflate cwnd using a mechanism known as "ACK Division" [SCWA99]. ACK Division consists of a receiver sending multiple ACKs for a single TCP data segment, each acknowledging only a portion of its data. A TCP that increments cwnd by SMSS for each such ACK will inappropriately inflate the amount of data injected into the network.

The core meaning of Section 3.1 of RFC 5681 is:

During slow start, for each ACK that cumulatively acknowledges new data, TCP increases cwnd by the number of acknowledged bytes, but by no more than SMSS (the sender's MSS) bytes.

This can be broken down into three key phrases:

  • for each ACK received: an ACK is the trigger.
  • cumulatively acknowledges new data: the ACK must cumulatively acknowledge new data.
  • cwnd += min (N, SMSS): N is the number of bytes newly acknowledged by the ACK, capped at the sender's MSS.

Why Is It Designed This Way?

The original text explains the reason as well:

This adjustment is part of Appropriate Byte Counting (ABC, RFC 3465), which makes TCP more robust against misbehaving receivers. An abnormal receiver might use a mechanism called ACK Division to induce the sender to inflate cwnd. In ACK Division, the receiver sends multiple ACKs for one TCP data segment, with each ACK acknowledging only a portion of that segment. If a TCP implementation increases cwnd by SMSS for every such ACK, it will inappropriately increase the amount of data injected into the network.

In short, RFC 5681 wants to prevent the receiver from tricking the sender into expanding its congestion window by “splitting ACKs.”

Suppose the sender transmits one data segment of size SMSS. Normally, the receiver should acknowledge the segment with one ACK. During slow start, the sender then increases cwnd by 1 SMSS, which is fine.

But if the receiver deliberately splits the acknowledgment into several small ACKs:

ACK 1: acknowledges the first 200 bytes
ACK 2: acknowledges the first 400 bytes
ACK 3: acknowledges the first 600 bytes
...

If the sender still follows the rule “increase cwnd by 1 SMSS for every ACK,” the same data segment will trigger multiple window increases. Only one segment was successfully transmitted through the network, but the sender behaves as though it can inject a great deal more data. cwnd is therefore inflated abnormally.

This is why RFC 5681 recommends:

cwnd += min(N, SMSS)

The meaning is:

  • If an ACK acknowledges only a small amount of new data, cwnd increases only by that amount.
  • If an ACK acknowledges a large amount of data, the increase for that ACK is still capped at 1 SMSS.

This preserves the normal slow-start behavior—one fully acknowledged MSS produces roughly one MSS of growth—while preventing ACK Division from maliciously inflating the window.

However, this is only the rule described by RFC 5681 / RFC 3465 from a byte-counting perspective. When we later look at the Linux kernel implementation, we will see a different viewpoint: Linux does not directly increase the window according to the number of newly acknowledged bytes. It counts the number of “fully acknowledged segments.” That difference is the most interesting part of this article.

Linux Kernel Implementation: Why Does It Look Different Again?

The source is in the Linux kernel's net/ipv4/tcp_cong.c; search for tcp_slow_start().

Here is the core function and the comment immediately before it:

/* Slow start is used when congestion window is no greater than the slow start
 * threshold. We base on RFC2581 and also handle stretch ACKs properly.
 * We do not implement RFC3465 Appropriate Byte Counting (ABC) per se but
 * something better;) a packet is only considered (s)acked in its entirety to
 * defend the ACK attacks described in the RFC. Slow start processes a stretch
 * ACK of degree N as if N acks of degree 1 are received back to back except
 * ABC caps N to 2. Slow start exits when cwnd grows over ssthresh and
 * returns the leftover acks to adjust cwnd in congestion avoidance mode.
 */
__bpf_kfunc u32 tcp_slow_start(struct tcp_sock *tp, u32 acked)
{
	u32 cwnd = min(tcp_snd_cwnd(tp) + acked, tp->snd_ssthresh);

	acked -= cwnd - tcp_snd_cwnd(tp);
	tcp_snd_cwnd_set(tp, min(cwnd, tp->snd_cwnd_clamp));

	return acked;
}

The comment contains a great deal of information. Here is a copy version so we can see it more clearly:

Slow start is used when the congestion window is no greater than the slow-start threshold. Linux is based on RFC 2581 and handles stretch ACKs correctly.

Linux does not strictly implement Appropriate Byte Counting (ABC) from RFC 3465. Instead, it uses another approach: a packet is counted as acknowledged only when it has been fully ACKed or SACKed. This defends against the ACK attacks described in the RFC.

For a stretch ACK with degree N, Linux's slow start treats it as though N ordinary ACKs of degree 1 had arrived back to back. ABC, however, caps N at 2.

When this growth would make cwnd cross ssthresh, slow start stops at the threshold and returns the unused ACK count to congestion avoidance so that congestion avoidance can continue adjusting the window.

Several terms need explanation first:

  • SACK: Selective Acknowledgment, which tells the sender which non-contiguous data blocks have already arrived.
  • (s)acked: the notation used in the kernel comment, meaning ACKed or SACKed.
  • stretch ACK: an ACK that acknowledges multiple segments at once instead of only one. For example, a receiver using delayed acknowledgment may wait for two or more TCP segments before sending one ACK.
  • degree N: this stretch ACK acknowledges N complete segments at once.

acked Is Not Measured in Bytes

The most important detail is that acked in this Linux function does not mean “how many bytes were acknowledged.” It means “how many complete segments were acknowledged.”

RFC 5681 / RFC 3465 tends to describe the rule in bytes:

cwnd += min(N, SMSS)

Here, N is the number of bytes newly acknowledged by the ACK.

But the implementation here is closer to:

cwnd += acked

Here, acked is the number of newly acknowledged complete segments. Linux itself maintains snd_cwnd in segment units, so + acked does not add a byte count directly to the window; it adds the number of complete segments acknowledged.

This explains why the kernel code looks different from the RFC formula:

  • RFC discussions often describe cwnd growth in bytes.
  • Linux's acked here is the number of fully acknowledged data segments.
  • Therefore, tcp_snd_cwnd(tp) + acked means that the window grows by the number of complete segments.

Under ideal conditions, this is equivalent to the textbook rule “for every ACK, cwnd += 1 MSS.” If an ACK acknowledges exactly one complete MSS, then acked = 1 and the window increases by one segment.

Why Does This Also Prevent ACK Division?

Linux's defense is different from the RFC's. It does not treat a fraction of a segment as one effective “complete-segment acknowledgment.” Only when a packet is fully acknowledged does it count toward acked. Therefore, even if a malicious receiver splits one segment into multiple small ACKs, acked cannot become multiple complete segments.

That is what the comment means when it says:

Linux does not strictly implement ABC, but does something “better.”

“Better” here can be understood as defending against ACK Division at the granularity of complete-segment acknowledgments rather than at byte granularity. This can provide higher throughput, avoids floating-point and byte-level calculations, and transitions more smoothly into congestion avoidance. The code walkthrough below will explain that transition line by line.

Linux Is More Aggressive with Stretch ACKs

Now consider a stretch ACK.

Suppose one ACK acknowledges three complete segments at once. Linux treats it as though three ordinary ACKs arrived consecutively. RFC 3465's ABC, by contrast, limits a single increase during slow start; its experimental recommendation says that L should not exceed 2*SMSS. Therefore, under a stretch ACK, Linux is somewhat more aggressive than ABC.

This also explains the comment:

Linux treats a stretch ACK that acknowledges N segments as N ordinary ACKs arriving back to back, while ABC limits that number to 2.

The Code in Detail: Reading tcp_slow_start() Line by Line

Let us return to the function:

__bpf_kfunc u32 tcp_slow_start(struct tcp_sock *tp, u32 acked)
{
	u32 cwnd = min(tcp_snd_cwnd(tp) + acked, tp->snd_ssthresh);

	acked -= cwnd - tcp_snd_cwnd(tp);
	tcp_snd_cwnd_set(tp, min(cwnd, tp->snd_cwnd_clamp));

	return acked;
}

First, several variables:

  • tp: the control block for the current TCP connection, containing the connection's congestion-control state.
  • tcp_snd_cwnd(tp): the current sender congestion window, measured in complete segments.
  • tp->snd_ssthresh: the slow-start threshold. Slow start grows only until approximately this threshold, after which congestion avoidance takes over.
  • tp->snd_cwnd_clamp: the hard upper limit for the congestion window, preventing cwnd from exceeding the maximum allowed by the system.
  • acked: the number of complete segments newly acknowledged by this ACK.

The first line:

u32 cwnd = min(tcp_snd_cwnd(tp) + acked, tp->snd_ssthresh);

calculates how far the window can grow during slow start:

new cwnd = min(current cwnd + newly acknowledged complete segments, slow-start threshold)

In other words, during slow start the window really does increase according to acked, but it cannot grow beyond ssthresh.

The second line:

acked -= cwnd - tcp_snd_cwnd(tp);

calculates how much of this ACK's acknowledgment count has already been consumed by slow start.

cwnd - tcp_snd_cwnd(tp) is the amount by which slow start actually increased the window this time. Subtracting that amount from acked leaves the acknowledgment count that slow start did not use.

What Happens When ssthresh Is Reached?

Consider this example:

current cwnd = 8
ssthresh = 10
acked = 5

Without the threshold, the window could grow from 8 to 13.

But slow start can only grow as far as ssthresh = 10:

actual new cwnd = min(8 + 5, 10) = 10

So slow start consumes only 2 of the 5 acknowledged segments:

actual growth = 10 - 8 = 2
remaining acked = 5 - 2 = 3

The third line:

tcp_snd_cwnd_set(tp, min(cwnd, tp->snd_cwnd_clamp));

actually updates snd_cwnd in the TCP control block. The value is also clamped against snd_cwnd_clamp, ensuring that the window does not exceed the system's configured upper limit.

The last line:

return acked;

returns the part of acked that slow start did not consume.

If slow start has not reached ssthresh, the function usually returns 0, meaning that the entire acknowledgment count was used to grow the slow-start window.

If this ACK crosses the slow-start threshold, the function returns the remaining acked so that the congestion-avoidance logic can use it. This prevents the portion of the same ACK that exceeds the slow-start threshold from being wasted; it is handed smoothly to congestion avoidance instead.

The Linux code can therefore be summarized as:

During slow start:
  cwnd grows by the number of newly acknowledged complete segments, acked;
  but it cannot grow beyond ssthresh;
  if this ACK reaches ssthresh, the leftover acked is passed to congestion avoidance.

This is why the formulas can look different after reading the RFC and then the Linux source: RFC 5681 / RFC 3465 describe the rule mainly in terms of acknowledged bytes, while Linux implements this function in terms of complete segments.

One Slow Start, Three Descriptions

The following table summarizes the comparison:

Dimension Textbook model RFC 5681 / RFC 3465 Linux kernel
Core viewpoint Build intuition Define protocol boundaries Engineering implementation
Growth basis Number of ACKs Bytes newly acknowledged by an ACK,N Complete segments newly acknowledged,acked
Slow-start formula Each ACK for a segment gives roughly+1 MSS cwnd += min(N, SMSS) cwnd += acked
Unit Usually abstracted in MSS Bytes Complete segments
Stretch ACK acknowledging 3 segments Usually not discussed RFC 5681: at most+1 SMSS; RFC 3465 ABC can tune L but not beyond 2*SMSS Approximately+3 segments
ACK Division defense Not covered Limit growth withmin(N, SMSS) Count only fully acknowledged segments inacked
Ideal one-ACK-per-packet case Roughly doubles within one RTT Roughly doubles within one RTT Roughly doubles within one RTT

As we can see, the textbook formula and the Linux implementation are equivalent for the idealized slow-start case. But there are many details and design considerations behind that similarity. If not for a classmate's one-sentence question, I might never have learned about them. If you know more about this topic, feel free to share it in the comments!

If you want to run an experiment yourself, you can refer to this Linux cwnd experiment.

  • RFC 3465: TCP Congestion Control with Appropriate Byte Counting

items.title: Behind localhost: A Network Journey That Never Leaves Home
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. Starting with a Familiar Address Type in a terminal and Vite cheerfully tells you that the service is running at ; click in a browser, and the page appears. Or, when working with Redis, you might run , which also connects to the local machine. We know this scene very well. Recently, however, while reviewing computer networks for the 408 exam, I started studying network layering again. That raised a natural question that is easy to overlook: If I am connecting to “myself,” does this still count as network communication? Does it really pass through the network protocol stack? If so, how many layers does it go through? A little investigation produced an answer that was slightly counterintuitive: yes, it counts, and it goes through quite a few layers. I wanted to write down the process from top to bottom and record what happens behind . In simple terms, it does not pass through a network card, switch, router, or cable the way an external request does. But inside the operating system, the application, transport, and network layers still do their jobs seriously. I used to think of as “one program directly chatting with another,” but it is more like a parcel that never leaves its residential compound: it never gets on the highway, but the shipping label, sorting, and delivery process still happen. One clarification first: is a name, not an IP address. It usually resolves to the IPv4 loopback address ; some systems may prefer the IPv6 address . To keep the route clear, the discussion below assumes the IPv4 loopback path through . Preface: Network Layering Before everything begins, let us briefly review the network layers from the 408 curriculum so that we have a framework for the analysis that follows. A short story first: The network layers are shown above. In 1977, the International Organization for Standardization ISO established a special committee to study a standard framework for network interconnection. It hoped to create a universal, open network-layering model so that any systems following the standard could communicate with one another. The reference model was formally published in 1984. It is the most standardized layering model, and almost any network can be fitted into it. The story of TCP/IP begins with the Advanced Research Projects Agency ARPA of the United States Department of Defense. In 1969, ARPANET was born. It was the predecessor of the modern Internet, initially intended to connect computers at universities and research institutions for resource sharing. In 1974, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published a paper on TCP. It introduced the concept of a “gateway”—which later evolved into the router—and solved the problem of connecting different networks. On January 1, 1983, ARPANET officially switched its core protocol from NCP to TCP/IP. This day is often regarded as the “birthday” of the modern Internet. Berkeley later integrated a free implementation of TCP/IP into Unix through BSD Unix. As Unix spread through universities and research institutions, TCP/IP quickly spread with it. Because TCP/IP was simpler, more efficient, and cheaper to implement, it naturally replaced the OSI approach and became today's dominant network-layering model. We will use the TCP/IP layers for the detailed discussion below. Before continuing, here is a quick summary of what the five TCP/IP layers do: The application layer is responsible for “what to say,” such as the HTTP, Redis, and MySQL protocols. The transport layer is responsible for “which process receives it and how it is delivered.” TCP and UDP live here, as do port numbers. The network layer is responsible for “which address to go to.” IP belongs here, so is a network-layer address. The link layer handles transmission over the same link. Ethernet frames and MAC addresses generally appear here. The physical layer turns bits into electrical, optical, or wireless signals and actually moves data through physical media. Based on that description, we can already analyze : is a port number belonging to the transport layer, while is an IP address belonging to the network layer. Once these two concepts are separated, many networking questions become much less confusing. TL;DR Layer What happens Key point --------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Application layer The browser or client sends an HTTP request to . This is where the data starts. Transport layer The operating system uses port to find the corresponding service process, such as your web server, and encapsulates the data in a TCP segment. The port number takes effect here. Network layer The operating system sees that the destination IP is , recognizes it as a loopback address , and hands it directly to the loopback interface instead of a physical network card. This is the crucial step: the data never leaves the machine. Link layer The loopback interface simulates a virtual link layer and pretends to send the data over a network, but in reality it only makes an in-memory turn. There is no real MAC-address exchange. Physical layer Skipped. No real hardware is involved, so the data is never turned into electrical or optical signals. This is the fundamental reason localhost is much faster than an external connection. So localhost actually completes most of the process; it simply skips the physical layer. Application Layer — No DNS Lookup Let us begin at the top and see what the first step of does. Experiment: External Host vs. Localhost In a terminal, I ran two commands: one accessing an external domain and one accessing my local service: I captured the traffic with tcpdump: When accessing the external domain, the terminal showed output like this: When accessing the local service, however, nothing appeared. That is because is not an ordinary domain name. Under the IETF standard RFC 6761 , it is reserved as a special hostname. When the operating system handles , it does not issue a DNS query; it reads the mapping directly from instead. You can verify this yourself: What Else Happens at the Application Layer? Once the address is resolved, curl has the destination . It then constructs an HTTP request: This request has exactly the same format as one sent to an external host. The header says , but that is merely a difference in content; the protocol behavior is identical. After constructing the request, curl writes it as a payload into the TCP socket associated with . The application layer's work is complete, and the data moves down to the next layer. Transport Layer — TCP Still Performs a Handshake Once the application layer writes the HTTP message into the TCP socket, the transport layer takes over. This differed from what I had initially imagined: Local communication still requires TCP's three-way handshake. TCP is a connection-oriented protocol. Whether the two endpoints are remote machines or two processes on the same machine, it still performs the complete handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. Only after the connection is established does the HTTP payload begin to travel. The only difference is that the handshake does not cross any physical line. It completes almost instantly inside the operating-system kernel through the loopback interface . The RTT approaches zero, so there are no retransmissions and no congestion-control episode—but the protocol state machine, sequence numbers, acknowledgment numbers, and port numbers are all still present. We can verify this with tcpdump. Open a terminal and listen on port 6370 of the loopback interface: Then run in another terminal. The output looks like this: Let us connect the lines one by one. Please first adjust the code block above to use horizontal scrolling so that the line details are easier to read. The Second Line: IPv6 Attempt Rejected The server on port 6370 was not listening on IPv6, so it immediately returned . This means that my service was bound to IPv4 , not to IPv6 . The Third Line: TCP Three-Way Handshake IPv4 curl switches to IPv4 , using source port . = SYN the client starts the connection . = SYN-ACK the server accepts the connection . = ACK the client confirms it . Notice the timestamps: all three lines are at , so the handshake completed within the same millisecond. The lines in between contain the HTTP request and response. The Sixth Line: TCP's Four-Way Termination The timestamps show just how quickly the process runs. Network Layer — Routing Keeps It on This Machine After the application layer passes the HTTP message to the TCP socket and the transport layer encapsulates it in a TCP segment, the data enters the network layer. Two things happen here: the IP header is added, and the routing table decides where the packet should go. We can inspect how localhost appears at the network layer with: The route destination for is itself, and the interface is ; the flags include . The route destination for an external IP is its corresponding network segment. Here the interface is not the physical network card , but , because I had a proxy service enabled; the flags include . Also note the MTU Maximum Transmission Unit . The local upper limit is the macOS-configured value of 16,384, while the connection to the external network uses the standard Ethernet limit of 1,500. Link Layer — A Virtual “Pretend Transmission” Once the network layer has made its routing decision, the packet is marked as “destined for this host.” In a normal network flow, the link layer would next encapsulate it in an Ethernet frame, fill in the destination MAC address, and hand it to the physical layer. For , however, things become unusual here. No Real MAC-Address Exchange We can verify this with the command: There is no output. For a loopback address, the operating system does not send an ARP request asking, “Who owns 127.0.0.1? Tell me your MAC address.” By contrast, if you look up another device on the local network: What Does the Loopback Interface Do? The operating system contains a special virtual network interface called the loopback interface, usually on macOS and Linux. You can see that it exists with: The key information is: : identifies this as a loopback interface. : shows that the address is bound to it. : the maximum transmission unit is much larger than Ethernet's 1,500. When the network layer decides to send a packet to , what actually happens is this: it hands the packet to the virtual interface . Instead of calling a network-card driver, directly “mirrors” the packet into the receive queue of the operating system's network stack. From the receiver's point of view, it looks as though a packet has arrived from the network. This process is called loopback inside the operating system. At its core, it is an in-memory copy, with no hardware involved. Does the Link Layer Still Exist? Strictly speaking, the link layer is responsible for “transmitting frames over the same link.” For the loopback interface, the operating system simulates an extremely simple link layer. It adds a fake link-layer header on macOS and on Linux , but it does not add real MAC addresses or perform CSMA/CD Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection . There is therefore no actual frame-transmission delay. What About the Physical Layer? It is skipped entirely. It is nice not to have to write this section at all ^∇^ The Answer: Localhost Passes Through Four of the Five TCP/IP Layers The only layer it skips is the physical layer. It is not as simple as “one program directly chats with another.” It still goes through the whole process of protocol encapsulation, port addressing, routing decisions, and interface scheduling. The only difference is that everything happens inside one machine—like a parcel that never leaves its residential compound: the label is attached, the parcel is sorted, and the delivery is signed for, but the courier never reaches the road.

The story of TCP/IP begins with the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) of the United States Department of Defense.

  • In 1969, ARPANET was born. It was the predecessor of the modern Internet, initially intended to connect computers at universities and research institutions for resource sharing.
  • In 1974, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published a paper on TCP. It introduced the concept of a “gateway”—which later evolved into the router—and solved the problem of connecting different networks.
  • On January 1, 1983, ARPANET officially switched its core protocol from NCP to TCP/IP. This day is often regarded as the “birthday” of the modern Internet.
  • Berkeley later integrated a free implementation of TCP/IP into Unix through BSD Unix. As Unix spread through universities and research institutions, TCP/IP quickly spread with it.

Because TCP/IP was simpler, more efficient, and cheaper to implement, it naturally replaced the OSI approach and became today's dominant network-layering model. We will use the TCP/IP layers for the detailed discussion below.

Before continuing, here is a quick summary of what the five TCP/IP layers do:

  • The application layer is responsible for “what to say,” such as the HTTP, Redis, and MySQL protocols.
  • The transport layer is responsible for “which process receives it and how it is delivered.” TCP and UDP live here, as do port numbers.
  • The network layer is responsible for “which address to go to.” IP belongs here, so 127.0.0.1 is a network-layer address.
  • The link layer handles transmission over the same link. Ethernet frames and MAC addresses generally appear here.
  • The physical layer turns bits into electrical, optical, or wireless signals and actually moves data through physical media.

Based on that description, we can already analyze localhost:8080: 8080 is a port number belonging to the transport layer, while 127.0.0.1 is an IP address belonging to the network layer. Once these two concepts are separated, many networking questions become much less confusing.

TL;DR

Layer What happens Key point
Application layer The browser or client sends an HTTP request to 127.0.0.1:8080. This is where the data starts.
Transport layer The operating system uses port 8080 to find the corresponding service process, such as your web server, and encapsulates the data in a TCP segment. The port number takes effect here.
Network layer The operating system sees that the destination IP is 127.0.0.1, recognizes it as a loopback address, and hands it directly to the loopback interface instead of a physical network card. This is the crucial step: the data never leaves the machine.
Link layer The loopback interface simulates a virtual link layer and pretends to send the data over a network, but in reality it only makes an in-memory turn. There is no real MAC-address exchange.
Physical layer Skipped. No real hardware is involved, so the data is never turned into electrical or optical signals. This is the fundamental reason localhost is much faster than an external connection.

So localhost actually completes most of the process; it simply skips the physical layer.

Application Layer — No DNS Lookup

Let us begin at the top and see what the first step of curl localhost:6370 does.

Experiment: External Host vs. Localhost

In a terminal, I ran two commands: one accessing an external domain and one accessing my local service:

curl -v http://markxu.icu
curl -v localhost:6370

I captured the traffic with tcpdump:

sudo tcpdump -i any port 53

When accessing the external domain, the terminal showed output like this:

12:26:00.381970 IP 198.18.0.1.56714 > public1.114dns.com.domain: 53233+ A? markxu.icu. (28)
12:26:00.382370 IP public1.114dns.com.domain > 198.18.0.1.56714: 53233* 1/0/0 A 198.18.0.172 (44)
12:26:00.387550 IP 192.168.20.80.49570 > pdns.dnspod.cn.domain: 13415+ AAAA? markxu.icu. (28)
12:26:00.387656 IP 192.168.20.80.63675 > public1.alidns.com.domain: 13415+ AAAA? markxu.icu. (28)
12:26:00.387763 IP 192.168.20.80.52301 > public1.alidns.com.domain: 41468+ A? markxu.icu. (28)
12:26:00.388014 IP 192.168.20.80.56763 > pdns.dnspod.cn.domain: 41468+ A? markxu.icu. (28)

When accessing the local service, however, nothing appeared. That is because localhost is not an ordinary domain name. Under the IETF standard (RFC 6761), it is reserved as a special hostname. When the operating system handles localhost, it does not issue a DNS query; it reads the mapping directly from /etc/hosts instead.

You can verify this yourself:

cat /etc/hosts | grep localhost

What Else Happens at the Application Layer?

Once the address is resolved, curl has the destination 127.0.0.1:6370. It then constructs an HTTP request:

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:6370
User-Agent: curl/8.7.1
Accept: */*

This request has exactly the same format as one sent to an external host. The Host header says localhost:6370, but that is merely a difference in content; the protocol behavior is identical.

After constructing the request, curl writes it as a payload into the TCP socket associated with 127.0.0.1:6370. The application layer's work is complete, and the data moves down to the next layer.

Transport Layer — TCP Still Performs a Handshake

Once the application layer writes the HTTP message into the TCP socket, the transport layer takes over. This differed from what I had initially imagined:

Local communication still requires TCP's three-way handshake.

TCP is a connection-oriented protocol. Whether the two endpoints are remote machines or two processes on the same machine, it still performs the complete handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client sends ACK. Only after the connection is established does the HTTP payload begin to travel.

The only difference is that the handshake does not cross any physical line. It completes almost instantly inside the operating-system kernel through the loopback interface lo. The RTT approaches zero, so there are no retransmissions and no congestion-control episode—but the protocol state machine, sequence numbers, acknowledgment numbers, and port numbers are all still present.

We can verify this with tcpdump. Open a terminal and listen on port 6370 of the loopback interface:

sudo tcpdump -i lo0 port 6370

Then run curl localhost in another terminal. The output looks like this:

tcpdump: verbose output suppressed, use -v[v]... for full protocol decode
listening on lo0, link-type NULL (BSD loopback), snapshot length 524288 bytes
14:17:36.505024 IP6 localhost.62464 > localhost.6370: Flags [S], seq 3529818479, win 65535, options [mss 16324,nop,wscale 6,nop,nop,TS val 2294771787 ecr 0,sackOK,eol], length 0
14:17:36.505080 IP6 localhost.6370 > localhost.62464: Flags [R.], seq 0, ack 3529818480, win 0, length 0
14:17:36.505206 IP localhost.62465 > localhost.6370: Flags [S], seq 1917119642, win 65535, options [mss 16344,nop,wscale 6,nop,nop,TS val 3300697293 ecr 0,sackOK,eol], length 0

Let us connect the lines one by one.

Please first adjust the code block above to use horizontal scrolling so that the line details are easier to read.

The Second Line: IPv6 Attempt (Rejected)

14:17:36.505024 IP6 localhost.62464 > localhost.6370: Flags [S], seq 3529818479, win 65535, options [mss 16324,nop,wscale 6,nop,nop,TS val 2294771787 ecr 0,sackOK,eol], length 0
14:17:36.505080 IP6 localhost.6370 > localhost.62464: Flags [R.], seq 0, ack 3529818480, win 0, length 0

The server on port 6370 was not listening on IPv6, so it immediately returned [R.]. This means that my service was bound to 127.0.0.1 (IPv4), not to ::1 (IPv6).

The Third Line: TCP Three-Way Handshake (IPv4)

14:17:36.505206 IP localhost.62465 > localhost.6370: Flags [S], seq 1917119642, win 65535, options [mss 16344,nop,wscale 6,nop,nop,TS val 3300697293 ecr 0,sackOK,eol], length 0
14:17:36.505344 IP localhost.6370 > localhost.62465: Flags [S.], seq 4137660183, ack 1917119643, win 65535, options [mss 16344,nop,wscale 6,nop,nop,TS val 4162405884 ecr 3300697293,sackOK,eol], length 0
14:17:36.505365 IP localhost.62465 > localhost.6370: Flags [.], ack 1, win 6380, options [nop,nop,TS val 3300697293 ecr 4162405884], length 0
  • curl switches to IPv4 (127.0.0.1), using source port 62465.
  • [S] = SYN (the client starts the connection).
  • [S.] = SYN-ACK (the server accepts the connection).
  • [.] = ACK (the client confirms it).

Notice the timestamps: all three lines are at 14:17:36.505, so the handshake completed within the same millisecond.

The lines in between contain the HTTP request and response.

The Sixth Line: TCP's Four-Way Termination

14:17:36.514408 IP localhost.62465 > localhost.6370: Flags [F.], seq 78, ack 1448, win 6358, options [nop,nop,TS val 3300697302 ecr 4162405893], length 0
14:17:36.514434 IP localhost.6370 > localhost.62465: Flags [.], ack 79, win 6379, options [nop,nop,TS val 4162405893 ecr 3300697302], length 0
14:17:36.514744 IP localhost.6370 > localhost.62465: Flags [F.], seq 1448, ack 79, win 6379, options [nop,nop,TS val 4162405894 ecr 3300697302], length 0
14:17:36.514791 IP localhost.62465 > localhost.6370: Flags [.], ack 1449, win 6358, options [nop,nop,TS val 3300697303 ecr 4162405894], length 0

The timestamps show just how quickly the process runs.

Network Layer — Routing Keeps It on This Machine

After the application layer passes the HTTP message to the TCP socket and the transport layer encapsulates it in a TCP segment, the data enters the network layer. Two things happen here: the IP header is added, and the routing table decides where the packet should go.

We can inspect how localhost appears at the network layer with:

route -n get 127.0.0.1

  • The route destination for 127.0.0.1 is itself, and the interface is lo0; the flags include LOCAL.
  • The route destination for an external IP is its corresponding network segment. Here the interface is not the physical network card en0, but utun1024, because I had a proxy service enabled; the flags include GATEWAY.

Also note the MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit). The local upper limit is the macOS-configured value of 16,384, while the connection to the external network uses the standard Ethernet limit of 1,500.

Link Layer — A Virtual “Pretend Transmission”

Once the network layer has made its routing decision, the packet is marked as “destined for this host.” In a normal network flow, the link layer would next encapsulate it in an Ethernet frame, fill in the destination MAC address, and hand it to the physical layer.

For 127.0.0.1, however, things become unusual here.

No Real MAC-Address Exchange

We can verify this with the arp command:

arp -a | grep 127.0.0.1

There is no output. For a loopback address, the operating system does not send an ARP request asking, “Who owns 127.0.0.1? Tell me your MAC address.”

By contrast, if you look up another device on the local network:

arp -a | grep 192.168

What Does the Loopback Interface Do?

The operating system contains a special virtual network interface called the loopback interface, usually lo0 on macOS and Linux. You can see that it exists with:

ifconfig lo0

The key information is:

  • LOOPBACK: identifies this as a loopback interface.
  • inet 127.0.0.1: shows that the address is bound to it.
  • mtu 16384: the maximum transmission unit is much larger than Ethernet's 1,500.

When the network layer decides to send a packet to 127.0.0.1, what actually happens is this: it hands the packet to the virtual interface lo0. Instead of calling a network-card driver, lo0 directly “mirrors” the packet into the receive queue of the operating system's network stack. From the receiver's point of view, it looks as though a packet has arrived from the network.

This process is called loopback inside the operating system. At its core, it is an in-memory copy, with no hardware involved.

Does the Link Layer Still Exist?

Strictly speaking, the link layer is responsible for “transmitting frames over the same link.” For the loopback interface, the operating system simulates an extremely simple link layer. It adds a fake link-layer header (NULL on macOS and LOOPBACK on Linux), but it does not add real MAC addresses or perform CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection). There is therefore no actual frame-transmission delay.

What About the Physical Layer?

It is skipped entirely. It is nice not to have to write this section at all (^∇^)

The Answer: Localhost Passes Through Four of the Five TCP/IP Layers

The only layer it skips is the physical layer.

It is not as simple as “one program directly chats with another.” It still goes through the whole process of protocol encapsulation, port addressing, routing decisions, and interface scheduling. The only difference is that everything happens inside one machine—like a parcel that never leaves its residential compound: the label is attached, the parcel is sorted, and the delivery is signed for, but the courier never reaches the road.
