items.title: Rejecting Reward Hacking: My Four Years at University
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. Over the past few days, I have said goodbye to one classmate after another. I stopped again and again at places I had passed countless times, looked around, and took many photos, reluctant to leave. I could not help looking back on my four years at university. Yet what kept returning to me was not only what I had done, but why I had made those choices at the time—and what might have been different if I could do it all again. To borrow a concept that has recently become popular: reject Reward Hacking, and refuse to turn your life into the maximization of a single metric. The previous few articles were all written around graduation—some were summaries from different angles, while others were simply scattered reflections. These four university years were undoubtedly the most vivid and consequential four of my twenty-two years of life. On the train leaving campus, I wrote this article to record the choices and experiences of those years, as a kind of private retrospective. Reward Hacking is originally a concept from reinforcement learning. It describes an agent exploiting loopholes in a reward function to obtain a higher reward in an unintended way. At university, that reward function easily becomes tied to GPA, class rank, recommendation-based postgraduate admission, scholarships, and competition awards. These things certainly matter, and in many contexts they genuinely demonstrate a student's excellence. But if they become the final objective and learning and growth themselves are forgotten, the result can easily turn into a real-life form of Reward Hacking. I did pay a small price over these four years for not having a higher GPA. If I could start again, perhaps I would strike a better balance. Even so, I want to record honestly what it felt like, in a meritocratic society where almost everyone is reminded to “optimize the metrics,” to rewrite my own reward function as: “Did I truly learn something? Do I understand society better? Am I closer to the person I wanted to become as a child?” This article is not meant to prove that I was right, because I still do not know the answer myself. It simply explains where I invested my time, how those choices shaped me, and leaves a trace of who I am now for my future self. Choosing to See the World Outside The 2022 gaokao—China's national college entrance examination—was certainly memorable. I received the worst ranking of my life. Students in my score range generally stayed within the province in order to attend a stronger university rather than studying farther away. After looking through many universities I had never previously heard of, I discussed the decision with my family. I still wanted to leave the province, see somewhere new, and experience life elsewhere. Fortunately, my family was very supportive. In the end, I went south to study in a city I had never visited before. Since I had decided to leave the province, I focused my university choices along China's southeast coast. We could submit up to ninety preferences that year; I filled in eighty-eight, divided into ambitious, realistic, and safe options. It was also the height of Zhang Xuefeng's popularity. Although the pandemic had hit the economy hard, people generally expected a rapid recovery and still made decisions according to pre-pandemic assumptions. Based on society's expectations at the time and my own interests, I selected several engineering disciplines related to computing and electronics. Predictably, every major that interested me became much more competitive than in previous years. None of my ambitious or realistic choices admitted me. Finally, at preference number fifty-four, the computer science program at Huaqiao University accepted me. Looking back, I do not regret that decision at all. Moving somewhere different from the environment in which I grew up, surrounded by classmates from cultural backgrounds unlike my hometown, was itself part of my university education. Under a more cautious evaluation system, perhaps I should have remained somewhere familiar and controllable, minimizing risk. But at the time, I felt that life should not be only about following an established path more efficiently. While I still had time and the cost of mistakes was low, I wanted to explore unfamiliar places. That was probably the first time I did not choose entirely according to the “optimal solution.” Trying to Pursue Something New When I arrived at university, most people around me still carried the mindset of high school. They wanted postgraduate recommendation places and high GPAs, and many senior students, parents, and teachers gave us the same advice. Indeed, a metric that can be quickly quantified and compared is the easiest way to display personal ability. Even after the gaokao, we had not escaped that logic. But after leaving high school, I wanted to try pursuing something new—something I truly wanted. I still cared about evaluation, of course. I simply did not want to keep living under the same reward function: maximize test scores in high school, maximize GPA and résumé value at university, then maximize salary and job level after graduation. Every step appears reasonable and efficient. But if we never stop to ask, “What are these metrics actually meant to serve?”, it is easy to surrender our real curiosity, sensitivity, and judgment while optimizing our way forward. Even in high school, I bought many university textbooks, including Chen Yuezen's General Biology and Fundamentals of Organic Chemistry , along with popular-science books about physics. I wanted to understand the knowledge I was studying and see whether there were deeper explanations, so I began teaching myself many subjects. These textbooks did not always help. University chemistry books, for example, had a fairly negative effect on my high-school grades. Their conclusions differed from the simplified conclusions taught in high school, and I would mix up the reasoning from the university texts. I overthought questions, worked more slowly, and often got them wrong. The signs were already there in high school. I paid little attention to “how to score more points on this particular test.” I simply believed that if I mastered the knowledge, the score would follow naturally. Only after the gaokao did I realize that, when it comes to examinations, understanding the subject is not enough; you must also understand why it is being tested. Only by mastering both can you score well. I had never considered the “why” behind the exam, so I wandered somewhat off course. Just after my first year began, my older cousin recommended csdiy and the Survival Guide for Shanghai Jiao Tong University. I began reading what people who had excelled under the gaokao evaluation system had written. Their ideas resonated deeply with me, and, with a somewhat adolescent sense of idealism, I wanted to become as ambitious and principled as they were. So I decided to spend less energy fighting over GPA points, learn more of what genuinely interested me, and explore some of society's overlooked corners. Writing this now, I cannot avoid wondering whether the decision “not to pursue GPA” reflected courage, or whether laziness was mixed into it as well. The important thing, however, is not the slogan but what I actually accomplished. Otherwise, simply rejecting one evaluation system only means falling into another, vaguer form of self-congratulation. Next, I want to talk about what I gained. Friendship: The People I Lived Alongside The most immediate benefit of not treating GPA as my only objective was my relationship with my classmates. I got along well with everyone in my class, and most of the time we had no direct conflicts of interest. We helped whenever we could and tried our best to share joy and experience it together. I gained several sincere friendships during university. Some classmates, partly influenced by me, began exploring their own interests, exercised with me, and attended symphony concerts. Together, we left many wonderful memories in the vast playground that was Xiamen. Through their experiences and hobbies, I also found my way into several circles, discovered more common interests, and spent a rich and comfortable university life. This mattered greatly to me. An intense evaluation system can easily turn everyone around us into an invisible object of comparison: his grade, her rank, who received an opportunity, and who earned one more bonus point. Over time, another person's success becomes a threat, while another person's failure becomes a source of reassurance. That is not a comfortable way to live. I am grateful that I did not remain trapped in that kind of relationship throughout university. My classmates were, first of all, people who shared their lives with me; they should not have been seen only as competitors blocking my path. Those relationships gave me people I could ask for help, joke with, eat with, and walk beside whenever I felt anxious. None of this fits neatly onto a résumé, yet it was one of the most genuine things I gained during those four years. Reading and Society: Widening My View of the World The second thing I gained was knowledge outside my major and the many books I read. I worked through part of Mankiw's Principles of Economics and tried reading the Selected Works of Mao Zedong and The Communist Manifesto . They made me recognize the distance between my own thinking and the ideals of a Communist Party member, while giving me a firmer position and a more flexible perspective. Because my classmates were interested in Japanese culture, I read several novels by Haruki Murakami and Yasunari Kawabata, along with The Chrysanthemum and the Sword , an American perspective on Japanese culture. Through them, I also watched a good deal of anime and became familiar with ACG culture. None of these things became a quantifiable achievement, but they genuinely made me less like a person who could only solve questions and complete assigned tasks. When meeting strangers, I could try to find shared topics and quickly establish common ground and interests. People need some apparently “useless” input before they can understand why others live as they do, why society operates as it does, and why they themselves become anxious, angry, or moved by public events. My third gain may have been contact with society. I rarely joined volunteer activities organized inside the university, nor did I participate in simple events just to accumulate volunteer hours and improve my postgraduate-recommendation prospects. Instead, I spent more time talking with people on the street, helping in local communities, and meeting people who were seriously building lives in Xiamen. I also met many peers who had not been as fortunate as I was in their educational opportunities but still worked hard in their own ways. Those experiences reduced much of my anxiety and internal exhaustion about society. Once I had seen specific people, many of the abstract, polarized stories endlessly fighting and belittling one another online became less absolute. Everyone was living in their own way: some fortunate, some struggling, some confused, some resilient. After meeting them, it became much harder to understand life as a simple ranking table, and I grew more confident that my chosen direction had something worthwhile in it. Contact with society was also good for my mental health. If someone understands themselves only through meritocracy's coordinate system, it is easy to remain forever “not good enough”: the university is not prestigious enough, the grades are not high enough, the project is not impressive enough, the family background is not distinguished enough, and the future is not certain enough. Real people are far more complex and abundant than those labels. As Chairman Mao once said: To struggle against Heaven is endless joy; to struggle against Earth is endless joy; to struggle with people is endless joy. Fitness: An Unexpected Gain I had always been overweight before university. Then, in the second semester of my second year of high school, I became desk mates with one of my best friends and suddenly lost around fifteen kilograms. He enjoyed working out, so I learned from him apparently I am quite accustomed to learning from the people around me, hehe . I have exercised ever since. Although I had trained for roughly four years by graduation, I still carried some extra fat and had not built an especially impressive physique. Yet the decision to exercise benefited me enormously and continues to make many parts of life easier. First, my physical condition improved, and I became less prone to illness and colds. Second, I gained strength: sometimes I could sit and play games for twenty-four hours straight, sleep once, and wake up refreshed rather than suffering terrible back pain. Most importantly, I learned about the body through training. Combined with what I had studied in high-school biology, I learned how different parts of daily life affect hormone secretion, developed reasonably good habits, understood what my body needed, avoided many overpriced pseudoscientific products, and maintained fairly good health. Fitness also introduced me to many friends in society. They came from different professions and carried very different experiences. I met students from different countries and regions through working out as well. From a utilitarian perspective, fitness can be packaged as discipline, image management, or a productivity tool. But a healthy body, a stable rhythm of life, genuine social connections, and moments spent training together are already part of one's quality of life. Their value is not that they let me stay awake longer in the next round of competition. They are about developing myself as fully as possible, caring for both mind and body. Competitions and Projects: Learning to Do Real Work Beyond the Results During my undergraduate years, I participated in several competitions. I learned the most from mathematical modeling competitions and from one Student Innovation Project. Beyond professional knowledge, the methods of teamwork left the deepest impression on me. Mathematical Modeling In a three-day mathematical modeling competition, we received a problem and had only three days to produce a complete paper. Whatever the circumstances, that was challenging. Even with AI, we still needed a basic understanding of the algorithms and had to analyze which methods suited the data before using AI-assisted programming to solve the actual problem. We disagreed many times along the way. I generally believed that problems like Questions A and B in the Mathematical Contest in Modeling, which required us to model and analyze real-world problems, were more challenging and interesting. I preferred those. But my teammates and I chose data-analysis problems in every official competition because we wanted the safer option, and I agreed that doing so gave us a much better chance of winning an award. As computer science students, we did not understand specialized physics as clearly as students in the relevant disciplines. Data-analysis questions overlapped more with our own knowledge: we usually applied several machine-learning algorithms, fit a plausible result, and wrote a paper around it. During competitions, we often stayed awake for two nights in a row, and emotional fluctuations were inevitable. As team leader, my main responsibilities were to keep everyone's emotions from damaging efficiency; complete the work according to our plan and division of responsibilities; determine the direction of our solution; use our familiarity with the relevant knowledge to develop an approach and convince my teammates why it best suited us; and, after mistakes, steer us back on course and prioritize solving the problem. I gradually figured these things out by reflecting on mistakes after making them. We abandoned our first mathematical modeling competition the day before submission. The main reason was that, as the person who had brought the team together, I had failed to lead. The other two classmates did not know each other well, so everyone felt awkward and hesitated to express their real thoughts. I understood similar lessons only after making each mistake once: the importance of communication, how to align progress quickly, how to change direction rapidly, and so on... Competitions are naturally driven strongly by metrics: awards, ratings, certificates, and bonus points in comprehensive assessments. But I later discovered that what remained was not the certificate. It was how to review a failure, move forward when a team disagreed, and help everyone continue trusting one another under enormous pressure. These abilities are not easily captured by a scoring rubric, but they are much closer to “doing real work.” Student Innovation Project: A First Taste of Research A senior student recommended the Student Innovation Project, saying I could learn a great deal from it. I contacted my undergraduate advisor on my own initiative, found a direction that both my teammates and I found reasonably interesting, finalized the project topic, and began a year-long research experience. At first, the work consisted mostly of documentation. It was my first time revising a project proposal over and over. Thanks to my advisor's patient guidance, I gradually learned how to communicate with a university supervisor—which required a very different relationship from talking with teachers in primary or secondary school—and how a standard formal document should be written. Throughout my two years of simple undergraduate research practice, I was deeply grateful to my advisor. In terms of teamwork, a year-long project with four students was considerably harder than a mathematical modeling contest. First, I needed to ensure that everyone genuinely learned knowledge they could use later. Second, as team leader, I should have selected the technology stack and direction promptly, organized offline activities so everyone could get to know one another, assigned responsibilities clearly, and checked progress regularly. I did none of those things well. Messages between us often went unanswered for one or two weeks, and our progress fell far behind that of other teams. Over the past few days, I have said goodbye to one classmate after another. I stopped again and again at places I had passed countless times, looked around, and took many photos, reluctant to leave. I could not help looking back on my four years at university. Yet what kept returning to me was not only what I had done, but why I had made those choices at the time—and what might have been different if I could do it all again. To borrow a concept that has recently become popular: reject Reward Hacking, and refuse to turn your life into the maximization of a single metric.

The previous few articles were all written around graduation—some were summaries from different angles, while others were simply scattered reflections. These four university years were undoubtedly the most vivid and consequential four of my twenty-two years of life. On the train leaving campus, I wrote this article to record the choices and experiences of those years, as a kind of private retrospective.

Reward Hacking is originally a concept from reinforcement learning. It describes an agent exploiting loopholes in a reward function to obtain a higher reward in an unintended way. At university, that reward function easily becomes tied to GPA, class rank, recommendation-based postgraduate admission, scholarships, and competition awards. These things certainly matter, and in many contexts they genuinely demonstrate a student's excellence. But if they become the final objective and learning and growth themselves are forgotten, the result can easily turn into a real-life form of Reward Hacking.

I did pay a small price over these four years for not having a higher GPA. If I could start again, perhaps I would strike a better balance. Even so, I want to record honestly what it felt like, in a meritocratic society where almost everyone is reminded to “optimize the metrics,” to rewrite my own reward function as: “Did I truly learn something? Do I understand society better? Am I closer to the person I wanted to become as a child?”

This article is not meant to prove that I was right, because I still do not know the answer myself. It simply explains where I invested my time, how those choices shaped me, and leaves a trace of who I am now for my future self.

Choosing to See the World Outside

The 2022 gaokao—China's national college entrance examination—was certainly memorable.

I received the worst ranking of my life. Students in my score range generally stayed within the province in order to attend a stronger university rather than studying farther away. After looking through many universities I had never previously heard of, I discussed the decision with my family. I still wanted to leave the province, see somewhere new, and experience life elsewhere. Fortunately, my family was very supportive. In the end, I went south to study in a city I had never visited before.

Since I had decided to leave the province, I focused my university choices along China's southeast coast. We could submit up to ninety preferences that year; I filled in eighty-eight, divided into ambitious, realistic, and safe options. It was also the height of Zhang Xuefeng's popularity. Although the pandemic had hit the economy hard, people generally expected a rapid recovery and still made decisions according to pre-pandemic assumptions. Based on society's expectations at the time and my own interests, I selected several engineering disciplines related to computing and electronics.

Predictably, every major that interested me became much more competitive than in previous years. None of my ambitious or realistic choices admitted me. Finally, at preference number fifty-four, the computer science program at Huaqiao University accepted me.

Looking back, I do not regret that decision at all. Moving somewhere different from the environment in which I grew up, surrounded by classmates from cultural backgrounds unlike my hometown, was itself part of my university education. Under a more cautious evaluation system, perhaps I should have remained somewhere familiar and controllable, minimizing risk. But at the time, I felt that life should not be only about following an established path more efficiently. While I still had time and the cost of mistakes was low, I wanted to explore unfamiliar places.

That was probably the first time I did not choose entirely according to the “optimal solution.”

Trying to Pursue Something New

When I arrived at university, most people around me still carried the mindset of high school. They wanted postgraduate recommendation places and high GPAs, and many senior students, parents, and teachers gave us the same advice. Indeed, a metric that can be quickly quantified and compared is the easiest way to display personal ability. Even after the gaokao, we had not escaped that logic.

But after leaving high school, I wanted to try pursuing something new—something I truly wanted. I still cared about evaluation, of course. I simply did not want to keep living under the same reward function: maximize test scores in high school, maximize GPA and résumé value at university, then maximize salary and job level after graduation. Every step appears reasonable and efficient. But if we never stop to ask, “What are these metrics actually meant to serve?”, it is easy to surrender our real curiosity, sensitivity, and judgment while optimizing our way forward.

Even in high school, I bought many university textbooks, including Chen Yuezen's General Biology and Fundamentals of Organic Chemistry, along with popular-science books about physics. I wanted to understand the knowledge I was studying and see whether there were deeper explanations, so I began teaching myself many subjects. These textbooks did not always help. University chemistry books, for example, had a fairly negative effect on my high-school grades. Their conclusions differed from the simplified conclusions taught in high school, and I would mix up the reasoning from the university texts. I overthought questions, worked more slowly, and often got them wrong.

The signs were already there in high school. I paid little attention to “how to score more points on this particular test.” I simply believed that if I mastered the knowledge, the score would follow naturally. Only after the gaokao did I realize that, when it comes to examinations, understanding the subject is not enough; you must also understand why it is being tested. Only by mastering both can you score well. I had never considered the “why” behind the exam, so I wandered somewhat off course.

Just after my first year began, my older cousin recommended csdiy and the Survival Guide for Shanghai Jiao Tong University. I began reading what people who had excelled under the gaokao evaluation system had written. Their ideas resonated deeply with me, and, with a somewhat adolescent sense of idealism, I wanted to become as ambitious and principled as they were. So I decided to spend less energy fighting over GPA points, learn more of what genuinely interested me, and explore some of society's overlooked corners.

Writing this now, I cannot avoid wondering whether the decision “not to pursue GPA” reflected courage, or whether laziness was mixed into it as well. The important thing, however, is not the slogan but what I actually accomplished. Otherwise, simply rejecting one evaluation system only means falling into another, vaguer form of self-congratulation.

Next, I want to talk about what I gained.

Friendship: The People I Lived Alongside

The most immediate benefit of not treating GPA as my only objective was my relationship with my classmates.

I got along well with everyone in my class, and most of the time we had no direct conflicts of interest. We helped whenever we could and tried our best to share joy and experience it together. I gained several sincere friendships during university. Some classmates, partly influenced by me, began exploring their own interests, exercised with me, and attended symphony concerts. Together, we left many wonderful memories in the vast playground that was Xiamen. Through their experiences and hobbies, I also found my way into several circles, discovered more common interests, and spent a rich and comfortable university life.

This mattered greatly to me. An intense evaluation system can easily turn everyone around us into an invisible object of comparison: his grade, her rank, who received an opportunity, and who earned one more bonus point. Over time, another person's success becomes a threat, while another person's failure becomes a source of reassurance. That is not a comfortable way to live.

My classmates were, first of all, people who shared their lives with me; they should not have been seen only as competitors blocking my path. None of this fits neatly onto a résumé, yet it was one of the most genuine things I gained during those four years.

Reading and Society: Widening My View of the World

The second thing I gained was knowledge outside my major and the many books I read.

I worked through part of Mankiw's Principles of Economics and tried reading the Selected Works of Mao Zedong and The Communist Manifesto. They made me recognize the distance between my own thinking and the ideals of a Communist Party member, while giving me a firmer position and a more flexible perspective. Those experiences reduced much of my anxiety and internal exhaustion about society. Once I had seen specific people, many of the abstract, polarized stories endlessly fighting and belittling one another online became less absolute. Everyone was living in their own way: some fortunate, some struggling, some confused, some resilient. Real people are far more complex and abundant than those labels. As Chairman Mao once said:

To struggle against Heaven is endless joy; to struggle against Earth is endless joy; to struggle with people is endless joy.

Fitness: An Unexpected Gain

I had always been overweight before university. Then, in the second semester of my second year of high school, I became desk mates with one of my best friends and suddenly lost around fifteen kilograms. Although I had trained for roughly four years by graduation, I still carried some extra fat and had not built an especially impressive physique. Most importantly, I learned about the body through training. Combined with what I had studied in high-school biology, I learned how different parts of daily life affect hormone secretion, developed reasonably good habits, understood what my body needed, avoided many overpriced pseudoscientific products, and maintained fairly good health.

Fitness also introduced me to many friends in society. They came from different professions and carried very different experiences. I met students from different countries and regions through working out as well.

From a utilitarian perspective, fitness can be packaged as discipline, image management, or a productivity tool. During my undergraduate years, I participated in several competitions. I learned the most from mathematical modeling competitions and from one Student Innovation Project. Beyond professional knowledge, the methods of teamwork left the deepest impression on me.

Mathematical Modeling

In a three-day mathematical modeling competition, we received a problem and had only three days to produce a complete paper. Whatever the circumstances, that was challenging. Even with AI, we still needed a basic understanding of the algorithms and had to analyze which methods suited the data before using AI-assisted programming to solve the actual problem.

We disagreed many times along the way. I preferred those. But my teammates and I chose data-analysis problems in every official competition because we wanted the safer option, and I agreed that doing so gave us a much better chance of winning an award. As computer science students, we did not understand specialized physics as clearly as students in the relevant disciplines. Data-analysis questions overlapped more with our own knowledge: we usually applied several machine-learning algorithms, fit a plausible result, and wrote a paper around it.

During competitions, we often stayed awake for two nights in a row, and emotional fluctuations were inevitable. As team leader, my main responsibilities were to keep everyone's emotions from damaging efficiency; complete the work according to our plan and division of responsibilities; determine the direction of our solution; use our familiarity with the relevant knowledge to develop an approach and convince my teammates why it best suited us; and, after mistakes, steer us back on course and prioritize solving the problem.

I gradually figured these things out by reflecting on mistakes after making them. We abandoned our first mathematical modeling competition the day before submission. Competitions are naturally driven strongly by metrics: awards, ratings, certificates, and bonus points in comprehensive assessments. But I later discovered that what remained was not the certificate. items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. My four years at university passed unbelievably quickly. It feels as though it was only yesterday that I first walked into the dorm as a freshman, met my roommates, and exchanged greetings with them. In the blink of an eye, it was already time to graduate. Xiamen is a beautiful city and an exceptionally comfortable place to live: its warm, humid climate; clean and orderly urban landscape; distinctive Minnan architecture; all kinds of greenery; bougainvillea blooming everywhere; and its broad, pristine bays... All of this made the city feel precious to me and made leaving difficult. My only regret was that, over those four years, I did not have more time and opportunities to wander through Xiamen and get to know it properly. To make up for that regret, I invited a classmate out for one more food crawl before graduation. We went looking for small shops with character and a personal touch. There were pleasant surprises, and there were disappointments too. All the photos were taken on a phone and left unedited, so please excuse the quality, haha. PuKu Fresh Doughnut Specialty Shop Opening hours: 10:30–20:00 Address: Near the Jimei Ancestral Temple, Jimei District Price: The mochi doughnuts we ordered were ¥15 each We had originally come at lunchtime for sour-cream curry, only to discover that the shop did not open until 14:30. With that plan foiled, we had no choice but to look elsewhere. On our way back, we suddenly noticed this inconspicuous little shop. It did not even have a large sign; we only stopped because a sidewalk board happened to mention doughnuts. The shop was spotless and almost minimalist, with mostly wooden furniture. It felt simple yet warm—an ideal place to sit for a while and take a couple of photos on a sunny day. As the saying goes, “Life is bitter, so have some mochi. Hello everyone, I am...” Ahem. We ordered two matcha mochi doughnuts and one preserved-plum guava mochi doughnut. The texture was genuinely excellent. The inside was remarkably elastic, while the shell was crisp. When I bit into it, I could feel the gluten pulling with a satisfying resilience, but it was calibrated perfectly and never became awkwardly chewy 🥲. The shell did not crumble everywhere like an ordinary pastry, either. Instead, it cracked naturally as the interior stretched and clung to the dough, making that combination of crispness and bounce unmistakable in every bite. The fillings deserve an even closer description 😋. On a hot day, the center felt wonderfully cool, with a rich texture like ice cream on the verge of melting, but none of the unpleasant iciness of frozen food. The matcha was intense without the usual tea astringency. The preserved-plum guava filling was more delicate, carrying the clean sweetness of ripe guava and tiny pieces of fruit. Pressing it against the roof of my mouth with my tongue revealed a surprisingly rich series of textures and flavors, although I could not really taste much of the preserved plum. The dough itself was only faintly sweet; almost all the sweetness came from the filling, where it served as a background note supporting the matcha and fruit aromas. Even after the filling was gone, the fragrance left in my mouth lasted long enough for me to enjoy the rest of the doughnut. Xiangkou Braised Beef Noodles Opening hours: 11:00–14:00, 17:00–21:00 Address: First floor of Xianghe Plaza, near Tuihua Park, Siming District Price: About ¥45 per person After finishing the mochi doughnuts, we immediately called a taxi into Xiamen Island and switched our plans to this beef-noodle shop. items.title: Why Do I Recommend College Students to Write Blogs?
items.content_text: After the gaokao, I came to a city 1,800 kilometers away from home for university. I walked out of the stage of life where exam scores were almost the only standard, and I encountered many things that made me start thinking. I also faced many choices that I had to make by myself. Sometimes one small thing would stay in my mind until midnight, repeating itself before sleep, leaving me with a stomach full of things to say. The next day, when I tried writing it down, I realized it was often just one or two short paragraphs of scattered thoughts, not much content at all. Writing helped me ease a lot of anxiety, and it also left clues for me to look back on later. Now when I turn back and read those records, I can clearly see how my worldview was pieced together from fragments of daily life. Writing a blog is a very good way to record these bits and pieces of life, making the origins of your thoughts traceable. As a College Student, What Can You Write About? The main audience of a blog is yourself. Many people do not write, and some are even afraid to write, because they think, "I'm not an expert, so nobody will read what I write." But the opposite is exactly why blogging is valuable. The most precious stage is precisely when you have not fully thought something through. Writing it down is itself a process of organizing your knowledge and the information you have. When writing, in order to express your thoughts, you gather related materials, check relevant content, and clarify the chain of logic. The goal is to squeeze that vague cloud floating in your mind into a visible shape. Actually, blogging does not have that many rules. You can record your hobbies, record the things that went wrong, and record the thoughts that make you feel "different" your "difference" is actually a clue and trace that helps people like you find you . You can also share your views on trending internet events. For example, regarding the recent popular "Jiahao" behavior, I feel it is a stage of life that may be embarrassing to look back on, but is still full of chaos and heat. Like the changes in adolescent thinking described in FLCL . There is no need to pick up a magnifying glass after growing up and start judging everything, suppressing the expression and emotions of teenagers who are still in adolescence. You can share knowledge you have learned: bugs and solutions from small projects you tinkered with, difficulties and challenges you encountered, how you completed an experiment, reflections after finishing a book, or experiences battling Linux. All of these can become small articles, like save points in life that you can come back to from time to time. How Do You Publish It After Writing? A blog is meant to be seen. Publishing it is like turning the sign at the door of a small shop to "OPEN," opening a door on the internet. Andy Matuschak calls this "working with the garage door up." Passersby glance inside, see you knocking things together, and naturally know someone is working here. If you have a bit of spare money, you can try buying your own domain name and use AI plus open-source projects to build a small website that fits your own taste. There are also many ready-made blog templates online. You can learn to adapt one, or directly deploy a site that belongs to you. If you do not want to deal with all that for now, you can simply write in any note-taking app and publish selected pieces to platforms with broad audiences, such as Zhihu, Bilibili, or WeChat Official Accounts. Good content will eventually find people willing to read it. As for things you do not publish publicly, you can keep them as your own archive, as clues to your thoughts. Looking back later is not a bad thing either. What Is a Good Blog Like? When it comes to what kind of blog counts as "good," I do not think you need to make it too complicated at the beginning. But there are a few points I want to talk about. The Audience of a Blog A blog is a public article once it is published, so you first need to consider the audience: who is reading it? Although I said earlier that the biggest audience of a blog is yourself, what you write should still have a certain public quality. It can be a place to clarify your own thoughts, but while you benefit from thinking and organizing, others should also be able to see something in it. The more professional and niche the topic is, the more you need to think about this. Of course, you can also use your blog like a "QQ Zone." Many bloggers dislike this concept and find it childish, but if your purpose is socializing and sharing, I do not think there is anything wrong with it. Through many similar personal blogs, I have seen the worries and joys of many peers like me. It feels like meeting a stranger who somehow becomes a friend. I think that is pretty nice. The Labeling of a Blog A blog should have its own theme. If a good blog wants to be remembered, it is best if people can easily attach a label to it. For example, when people want news analysis, philosophy reading notes, historical explanations, economic changes, or technical blogs, they can immediately think of whose website to visit. But this requirement is a bit too high for a college student. A normal college student, after coming out of the gaokao experience, usually does not have much life experience, deep reading, or even a writing habit beyond the style of exam essays. That is completely normal. When you have fewer topics to choose from, you can write as much as you can and record many aspects of your life. At this stage, you can use category management so that readers who need specific content can filter things simply. They can block out your daily fragments and focus only on your main output. This may be a passable solution. After you accumulate enough experience, it is not too late to open a dedicated column. I partly refer to the ideas of the 2750words blogger. I agree with most of his philosophy, though perhaps our life stages are different, or our entry points into blogging are different. I think a blog should still be centered on the blogger. Since it is already a personal blog, it is unreasonable to let someone else's design philosophy decide everything. If you do not like a website, you can simply choose not to read it. There will always be people who do like it. Just keep your own strong authorial presence. After all, the owner of the blog is you. Comfort will always matter more than being "correct." The Word Count of a Blog There should be some limit to word count. Many people do not like reading overly long articles, or rather, overly verbose articles. If a simple matter is hard to explain in fewer words, it probably means the writing is not clear enough yet. Verbose but unclear expression is a big problem. My advisor once gave me a requirement: "Your writing should have key points, so readers can roughly understand the intention within 30 seconds. It should have a two-minute reading path and a five-minute reading path." Proper bold text and well-designed section headings are fairly good ways to solve this problem. A Rational Discussion: Benefits and Costs I have said many things above, and it may sound like writing a blog is a "guaranteed profitable" deal. But if I do not tell you the corresponding costs and price, that would feel a little irresponsible. Writing a blog is not a social shortcut. It is more like opening a quiet little shop that few people visit. A good blog is a good way to speak on the internet. What you write represents the things you care about and the way you think about problems. But this does not automatically bring traffic, make your personal brand explode, make important people suddenly discover you, or bring opportunities on its own. Most of the time, blogging is slow cultivation by one person. From a personal perspective, maintaining and persisting with a blog is not something everyone can do. I have seen too many blogs disappear after the first three or five posts, sometimes even with the domain name no longer renewed. To be honest, I am also still in that "three-minute enthusiasm" stage, and future updates probably will not be as frequent as they are now. Also, "being misunderstood is the fate of anyone who expresses themselves." If you are sensitive, you will pay some emotional cost. Maintaining a website also requires continuous financial input. How it develops later is indeed hard to say. Blogging, as an activity that has already declined, does not bring many direct returns. We are now in the era of new self-media. Making videos and short videos is a more popular and mainstream choice. With platform support, there is more traffic and more visibility. Considering so many disadvantages, why do I still recommend it? First, as discussed earlier, writing articles is, so far, the fastest form of output, the one that most forces you to think, and the one that exposes logic most directly . What is truly valuable is the thought behind the words. Writing can greatly train a person's ability to think. Second, as a flexible form of output with low time cost, low storage cost, and a low entry threshold, writing has the highest cost-performance ratio among output-oriented hobbies. Pure text publishing is supported by many platforms, and a good article can be lightly modified into a video script, serving as the foundation for other forms of output. Create Boldly The confusion, awkwardness, sudden happiness, and unexplained sadness we are experiencing now are all gifts that belong uniquely to this stage of life. When we look back later, perhaps we will be grateful that we once made the decision to lay out our thoughts and record them. After all, in this empty space of the internet, only when you keep a light on will someone follow that light and come over to say: "Hey, I am here too." I am not sure how far this light can shine, nor how long it can stay lit. I simply believe that some things do not need to prove they are worth starting before they become worth starting.

Through many similar personal blogs, I have seen the worries and joys of many peers like me. It feels like meeting a stranger who somehow becomes a friend. I think that is pretty nice.

The Labeling of a Blog

A blog should have its own theme. If a good blog wants to be remembered, it is best if people can easily attach a label to it. For example, when people want news analysis, philosophy reading notes, historical explanations, economic changes, or technical blogs, they can immediately think of whose website to visit.

But this requirement is a bit too high for a college student. A normal college student, after coming out of the gaokao experience, usually does not have much life experience, deep reading, or even a writing habit beyond the style of exam essays. That is completely normal. When you have fewer topics to choose from, you can write as much as you can and record many aspects of your life. At this stage, you can use category management so that readers who need specific content can filter things simply. They can block out your daily fragments and focus only on your main output. This may be a passable solution. After you accumulate enough experience, it is not too late to open a dedicated column.

I partly refer to the ideas of the 2750words blogger. I agree with most of his philosophy, though perhaps our life stages are different, or our entry points into blogging are different. I think a blog should still be centered on the blogger. Since it is already a personal blog, it is unreasonable to let someone else's design philosophy decide everything. If you do not like a website, you can simply choose not to read it. There will always be people who do like it. Just keep your own strong authorial presence. After all, the owner of the blog is you. Comfort will always matter more than being "correct."

The Word Count of a Blog

There should be some limit to word count. Many people do not like reading overly long articles, or rather, overly verbose articles. If a simple matter is hard to explain in fewer words, it probably means the writing is not clear enough yet. Verbose but unclear expression is a big problem. My advisor once gave me a requirement: "Your writing should have key points, so readers can roughly understand the intention within 30 seconds. It should have a two-minute reading path and a five-minute reading path." Proper bold text and well-designed section headings are fairly good ways to solve this problem.

I have said many things above, and it may sound like writing a blog is a "guaranteed profitable" deal. But if I do not tell you the corresponding costs and price, that would feel a little irresponsible.

Writing a blog is not a social shortcut. It is more like opening a quiet little shop that few people visit. A good blog is a good way to speak on the internet. What you write represents the things you care about and the way you think about problems. But this does not automatically bring traffic, make your personal brand explode, make important people suddenly discover you, or bring opportunities on its own. Most of the time, blogging is slow cultivation by one person.

From a personal perspective, maintaining and persisting with a blog is not something everyone can do. I have seen too many blogs disappear after the first three or five posts, sometimes even with the domain name no longer renewed. To be honest, I am also still in that "three-minute enthusiasm" stage, and future updates probably will not be as frequent as they are now. Also, "being misunderstood is the fate of anyone who expresses themselves." If you are sensitive, you will pay some emotional cost. Maintaining a website also requires continuous financial input. How it develops later is indeed hard to say.

Blogging, as an activity that has already declined, does not bring many direct returns. We are now in the era of new self-media. Making videos and short videos is a more popular and mainstream choice. With platform support, there is more traffic and more visibility.

Considering so many disadvantages, why do I still recommend it?

First, as discussed earlier, writing articles is, so far, the fastest form of output, the one that most forces you to think, and the one that exposes logic most directly. What is truly valuable is the thought behind the words. Writing can greatly train a person's ability to think. Second, as a flexible form of output with low time cost, low storage cost, and a low entry threshold, writing has the highest cost-performance ratio among output-oriented hobbies. Pure text publishing is supported by many platforms, and a good article can be lightly modified into a video script, serving as the foundation for other forms of output.

Create Boldly

The confusion, awkwardness, sudden happiness, and unexplained sadness we are experiencing now are all gifts that belong uniquely to this stage of life. When we look back later, perhaps we will be grateful that we once made the decision to lay out our thoughts and record them. After all, in this empty space of the internet, only when you keep a light on will someone follow that light and come over to say: "Hey, I am here too."

I am not sure how far this light can shine, nor how long it can stay lit. I simply believe that some things do not need to prove they are worth starting before they become worth starting.
items.summary: Although the idea of writing blogs already feels a little outdated, I still recommend it. It helps you clarify your thoughts, record the process of growing up, and maybe even meet like-minded people along the way.

items.title: Looking at AI Through the Lens of Meme: Thoughts After Playing Death Stranding 2
items.content_text: Recently I finished the story of Death Stranding 2 . The abstractness of some of its performances shocked me. I could not understand why certain scenes were designed that way: why did people suddenly start singing here? Why did the villain perform the American national anthem at the end? And why was pizza kung fu so powerful? After doing some quick research, I suddenly realized something: this kind of game seems very hard to copy. Not only because of its gameplay, but even more because of its cultural expression. What Kind of Game Is Death Stranding? Unlike the game genres already on the market, it has its own new gameplay experience and worldview. It is not like the Assassin's Creed series, which has already formed a relatively mature AAA industrial template: a big open world, repeated outpost clearing, RPG-style equipment growth, question marks all over the map the question marks in The Witcher 3 were still pretty good , and static story cutscenes. It feels as if, as long as the budget, team, and production pipeline are big enough, you can make something that "looks about right" though I heard Ubisoft is remaking Black Flag, so I will still have to try it on hands . It is also not like Soulslikes, which have a very clear gameplay skeleton: bonfires, death penalties, stamina bars, boss design, fragmented narrative. Change the worldview and art theme, and players can quickly understand, "Oh, this has some Souls flavor." Nor is it like a linear AAA game that gives you as many cinematic shocks and exquisite level designs as possible within a limited route. Death Stranding is different. Its gameplay is new, its game concept is something I have never seen before, and the pleasure it brings has a very distinctive taste. Others can imitate its art, its long takes, its barren, absurd, realistic, or slightly mystical atmosphere. They can even make an identical "delivery game" or "infrastructure-building game." But it is very hard to truly reproduce the feeling it gives players. Because the core of the game is not a single system, but a complete experience: walking through the wilderness with cargo, planning routes, keeping balance, completing asynchronous cooperation or confrontation with strangers , slowly stepping out a path on what used to be a barren and rugged wasteland, all inside a self-consistent and rich worldview, in a work that has its own philosophical discussion and ideological expression. Games are interactive art, so let's talk about gameplay. If we only talk about gameplay, it seems a little boring. What it focuses on is the worst part of almost every open-world game: walking time. Most game companies keep optimizing fast travel so players do not spend too much time on the road and get tired. But Death Stranding makes this its main selling point. The game is basically about delivering cargo from A to B. Yet once you truly get into it and quietly sync with the game's wavelength, you find a strong stickiness inside this "boredom": climbing steep mountains, sneaking through watcher territory, drawing out and defeating BTs, building infrastructure along the road to make later deliveries easier, and finally delivering cargo to an NPC with zero damage, receiving likes and blueprints for new equipment. Everything you do on this journey, including the path you walk, can be synchronized into another player's world: maybe your infrastructure helps someone else, or maybe the simplest thing you leave behind is just telling others that this route can reach the destination. During the process, you feel the joy of getting new equipment and the sense of achievement that comes from forming "connections" with other players. Its worldview also reaches a clever kind of balance. Timefall, umbilical cords, the Beach, the chiral network: a series of new terms and settings relate to each other while also corresponding to meanings in the real world, creating certain metaphors that make the world easier to understand and enter let me complain here about the long-winded text and so-called "setting terms" in some gacha games . All settings participate in the difficulties and challenges players encounter: some as special mechanics, some as final goals, and some as potential dangers that need to be guarded against. Meanwhile, Kojima-san also adds many Easter eggs into this world, or you could say "humorous and abstract" content, just like the performances I mentioned at the beginning. At first they made me wonder: won't this break the carefully designed worldview? For such a high-budget AAA game, is it not too risky for the director to smuggle in so much personal taste? But the result is just like the line circulating online: "Commercialization is under pressure, and finally yielded to Hideo Kojima." For casual players, these moments bring a knowing smile during the game. But if you dig into them carefully, you find that they not only do not break the worldview, but add another layer of metaphor and philosophical thought to it. The appropriately abrupt feeling hooks players into thinking. While feeling surprised, they can also experience the corresponding meaning. Whether you understand it or not, you slowly accept this abruptness, and it becomes one of the game's unique features. So I started to wonder: what kind of game creator is Hideo Kojima exactly? Why does he have so many fans around the world? Why does he dare to invest so much money into making a game that looks "not in line with the blockbuster formula"? Why was the first game so divisive when it first came out, while by the second one, many players could already seriously discuss it as a Game of the Year candidate? What Meme Means With this curiosity, I watched some Death Stranding 2 lore analysis videos on Bilibili and read some interviews with Hideo Kojima. I learned about a turbulent life experience full of misfortune and coincidence, one that carries the shadow of many otaku boys. I also learned how movies, games, reading, and thinking inspired his creative career. One interview especially caught my attention: when talking about his first directed work, Metal Gear , he said it mainly explored Meme. When I first saw the word, my immediate reaction was: how could "meme images" have been a subject of discussion nearly forty years ago? After all, in today's internet context, the most common Chinese translation of "meme" is basically "funny image template": cats and dogs with captions, reaction images, abstract templates. They all seem to count as memes. But the Meme Kojima was talking about was clearly not that. So I looked it up. According to the Wikipedia entry on Meme, the concept of the meme comes from Richard Dawkins's 1976 book The Selfish Gene . Dawkins wanted to express that culture also has units of transmission similar to genes. A meme can be a melody, an idea, a slogan, a fashion, a skill, or any cultural fragment that people imitate, copy, transform, and continue spreading. In other words, a meme was not originally an internet reaction image. Reaction images are certainly memes, but memes are much bigger than reaction images. Our two-part allegorical sayings are memes, idioms are memes, books are memes, movies are memes, internet catchphrases are memes, collective repetition in Bilibili comments is a meme, gamer slang is a meme you are not qualified, you are not qualified, and because of that you are not qualified , and even certain creative methods, aesthetic tastes, and narrative formulas are memes. Like genes inside culture, they are copied, rewritten, sometimes misunderstood, then recreated by generation after generation, and they keep living. AI Cannot Create Cultural Genes After understanding what meme means, and then thinking about the story design and hidden metaphors behind Death Stranding 2 , I could not help connecting it to the hottest concept of our era: AI. Suddenly, the whole thing became interesting to me. Today's large language models are not truly people with lived experience. They do not have blurry childhood memories, the joy of staying up all night playing games, the surprise of walking into the wilderness for the first time, or the feeling of being struck by a lyric or a melody late at night while emo. In essence, they are huge probability calculators, absorbing a vast amount of text, images, code, music, and knowledge left behind by humans, then searching for vector relationships among those existing materials and giving an answer that is "most like something a human would say." In other words, through a massive amount of human corpus, AI has already become very good at using existing memes. Ask it to write a cyberpunk story, and it knows how neon lights, rainy nights, prosthetic bodies, monopolistic corporations, and lower-class districts should be combined. Ask it to design a Soulslike game setting, and it knows roughly what ruined kingdoms, lost gods, curses, bosses, and obscure item descriptions should look like. Ask it to make an "internet-style" image, and it also knows the common templates in contemporary aesthetics. But the problem is that most of this is still calling, stitching, and redistributing existing cultural genes. AI can quickly rearrange the familiar things we already know, sometimes beautifully, completely, and convincingly. But New Cultural Currents Often Come from Bold Attempts and Mistakes Looking back at new cultural currents in human history, quite a few impressive ones came from a bold attempt, a misunderstanding, or simply an accident. Take the Renaissance as an example. Some ancient Greek and Roman knowledge of philosophy, literature, art, and science had been preserved, filtered, and used by the Church for theological purposes during the Middle Ages, partly to consolidate its rule and class structure. During the Renaissance, humanists such as Petrarch and Boccaccio rediscovered a large number of classical texts from the Arab world and monasteries. But they did not simply restore them in a fundamentalist way. Instead, they interpreted them through the eyes and needs of their own time . They emphasized the praise of human reason, secular life, and bodily beauty in classical culture, while to some extent ignoring or downplaying the superstition, slavery, and pessimism that also existed in antiquity. This created a historical and cultural explosion. Even Confucianism, which we now sometimes criticize as part of feudal tradition, was also an incredibly rebellious existence in its own social context. AI only produces something that is highly likely to be correct based on existing memes, or cultural content. The difference already appears at the level of underlying logic. So if you ask whether it can create a truly new meme, whether it can continuously create a new mode of expression, a new structure of experience, or a new "cultural gene" that humans will understand from then on, I still feel somewhat doubtful. That brings me back to why the performance arrangements and gameplay design of Death Stranding feel so precious to me. It does not simply invite Hollywood actors, shoot a pile of luxurious cutscenes, and then stuff them into an open-world gameplay loop everyone already knows. It did invite recognizable actors such as Norman Reedus, Léa Seydoux, and Mads Mikkelsen, and it does have cinematic shots, music, and narrative ambition. But it does not treat these things merely as gimmicks to make money. Instead, it uses a very strange, risky, and unstable gameplay system to push a new experience in front of players. "Delivery" is such an ordinary thing, even boring-sounding. But in Death Stranding , it becomes a way of connecting people. What you carry is not just cargo, but also weight, responsibility, route choice, risk, and time. A bridge you build may be used by another player you will never meet. A charging station you place may just happen to save a desperate player. The game's "connection" is not a line of dialogue. It is built into terrain, physics, resources, and asynchronous multiplayer systems. Even when I continued building facilities later, I started thinking about whether this device would still help other players after entering their worlds. This feels very much like the birth of a new meme. Before it, it was hard to imagine that a big-budget game could turn "walking" and "delivery" into the core experience. After it, whenever people see similar asynchronous assistance or confrontation, they may say: "This feels a bit like Death Stranding." That sentence itself shows that it has already become a cultural unit that can be recognized, quoted, and spread. From now on, there are two kinds of people in the world: those who have not played Death Stranding , and those who have. As for the bizarre performance effects mentioned earlier, I think it is precisely these bizarre performances that, in return, become strange memes. They give this distinctive game an additional kind of "connection" with other cultures and fans, and create new memes belonging to its own players, like a secret key for connection among the game's fans. From Another Angle, the Relationship Between AI and Meme May Not Be So Pessimistic If AI only keeps repeating old memes, then of course it will make culture more average, more similar, more "correct but boring." We can already see this flavor in many places: copy that is as pretty as a template but stiff, images that are as polished as templates but incomplete, and expressions that are fluent but lack personal experience. They are not bad, but they are also unlikely to leave long-lasting traces. But from the opposite direction, AI may also become a tool that helps memes keep growing. In the past, when someone had a strange idea and wanted to turn it into a game, animation, software, short film, or other cultural work, they often needed a lot of money, a team, technical accumulation, or the ability to absorb trial-and-error costs. Many ideas were not worthless; they died before they could land. Modeling, programming, art, sound effects, editing, testing: these are not merely "repetitive labor," but they really are high walls that must be crossed before an idea becomes a work. If AI continues to develop and can truly reduce costs in modeling, code, animation, scripts, level prototypes, and other parts of the process, letting more people bring their ideas into reality with smaller teams, less money, and shorter trial-and-error cycles, then that might be a beautiful thing. My own little website also developed this quickly and gained this many effects precisely because of AI. Because culture is not created only by big companies and big budgets. Many new memes may begin as one person's strange thought, a small team's obsession, a gameplay idea that does not look very commercial, or a simple sentence: "I just want to try whether this works." If AI can drag these thoughts out of people's heads and into reality, allowing more works that previously had no chance to take shape to be seen, then it is not replacing culture. It is widening the entrance through which culture can happen. Of course, the premise is that we still provide something truly human. AI can help us reach the work faster. But new memes may still have to grow out of human loneliness, curiosity, stubbornness, failure, and experience. The inspiration Death Stranding 2 gave me is probably this: when a creator truly presses their feelings, aesthetics, and sense of problems into a work, it has the chance to become a new cultural gene. At first, people may find it strange, alternative, or unlike a "normal game." But as long as it really strikes something, it will be remembered, discussed, imitated, or misunderstood, and then it will keep spreading. Finally, I want to use the closing words Hideo Kojima gives to players in Death Stranding 2 to look toward our future and development in the AI era. Even if we do not know what the future will be like, we should not stop exploring, and we should not stop trying. Though the future is a product of every present that precedes it, Tomorrow does not belong to today. To live is to imagine ourselves in the future. And there we inevitably arrive Yet our place in said future may not be the one we envision. -- Kobo Abe, The Search for the Present

Though the future is a product of every present that precedes it,

Tomorrow does not belong to today.

To live is to imagine ourselves in the future.

And there we inevitably arrive

Yet our place in said future may not be the one we envision.

-- Kobo Abe, The Search for the Present
