items.title: From Student Innovation Project to Graduation Thesis: How My Research Thinking Evolved
items.content_text: After finishing my graduation project, I kept wanting to write a blog post about it. I do not want to rewrite my thesis abstract. If I did that, it would be better to just read the thesis. What I want to record is how the project actually grew: at first it did not even have a clear direction. It was only an ordinary attempt to ask my advisor whether there was a suitable project I could join. Later, step by step, it became a student innovation project, a system, an algorithm, and finally my undergraduate graduation thesis. Looking back now, the most interesting part is not that I eventually built some amazing model or algorithm implementation. It is that I clearly felt, for the first time, that failure in research or engineering is not a full stop. It is a concrete signpost, telling me where to go next. The Starting Point: A Challenge In the second semester of my sophomore year, I went to my undergraduate advisor and asked whether there was any project suitable for me to participate in, partly because a senior strongly recommended that I try applying for a student innovation and entrepreneurship project. At that time, I did not have a clear idea of "medical imaging" yet. My understanding of "segmentation" was still roughly: circle out a certain region in an image, just like those classic YOLO examples from introductory computer science courses. My advisor introduced me to the PENGWIN 2024 pelvic fracture segmentation challenge, and asked me to first try exploring around this competition. PENGWIN's task is very intuitive, and also very difficult: given CT or X-ray data from patients with pelvic fractures, let an algorithm automatically segment the fracture fragments. The public description mentions why this type of task is hard: the pelvis has a complex structure; fracture fragments vary greatly in shape and location; and fracture surfaces often become blurry due to collision, compression, and adhesion. This was already close to the frontier of the field. For a complete beginner like me, it was extremely hard to even get started, not to mention that I still had ambitions to make something "innovative." The training set for PENGWIN Task 1 on Zenodo contains 100 CT cases with labels. The full dataset comes from 150 patients, with 50 cases reserved as the official test set for final scoring. The data clearly annotates the sacrum, left and right hip bones, and their fragments, with detailed descriptions. It was an ideal dataset. Back then, I did not truly feel the weight of those difficulties. My first reaction was more like: since there is data, a competition, and a task, let's build the system first. And so the student innovation project that "tortured" me for a whole year began. That year, several teammates and I built a basic medical management system. The system itself needed to handle data management, model invocation, and result visualization. It sounded like a complete project, and in practice it really did take a lot of time. Frontend, backend, data flow, model APIs: many things were written while searching, rewritten while learning, and overturned while building. Very often we worked until four or five in the morning before realizing we really had to rest. The hardest part of the whole process was team collaboration: explaining task requirements, expected outcomes, and so on. That development experience with teammates also exhausted me quite a lot maybe I will write another article about that later, but it is not the focus this time . By the midterm stage, the system finally had a basic shape, but my advisor pointed out a more important issue: the system could display results, but our medical image segmentation algorithm also needed innovation. Directly using other people's work was not enough for a student innovation project. That sentence hurt a bit. After slowly grinding out the system, it is easy to mistakenly believe that most of the work is already done, at least because the visible workload is clear. But in medical image segmentation, the interface only "serves the result." The truly difficult part is where the result comes from. And that hidden workload is much harder to explain clearly to others. My First U-Net, and My First Failure That was when I officially started filling in my knowledge of medical image segmentation. Naturally, the first thing I could not avoid was U-Net. It is a classic encoder-decoder structure in medical image segmentation. One side downsamples to extract semantic information, the other side upsamples to recover spatial details, and skip connections bring shallow texture information back in between. It did not sound too complicated, so I naturally developed a naive confidence: then I will write one myself. So I hand-wrote my first U-Net. Looking back now, that was probably one of the most educational pieces of code I have ever written. The model could run, the loss would drop, and the results could be visualized. Seeing my GPU fully occupied, the terminal reporting a new round of training information, and the loss curve slowly going down was honestly a very happy thing. But the results were still poor. Later, I tried adding small modules such as depthwise separable convolutions, spatial-channel dual attention, and SE blocks. At that stage, I had read very few papers. More often, I picked things from existing modules that "looked possibly useful," stuffed them into the network, and then listened to AI's flattery, feeling that I had done a decent job. The results did not suddenly improve just because there were more modules. There was some improvement, but still not enough. What was more brutal was that it still could not beat the competition baseline. That hit me hard. I had spent a year building the system, modifying the model, staying up late for months, and even abandoning fitness I was genuinely afraid of sudden death , but the final algorithmic effect was not ideal. That was the first time I realized deep learning does not automatically become stronger by stacking a few "advanced modules" together. Especially in medical imaging, data volume, annotation strategy, preprocessing, loss functions, post-processing, and evaluation metrics may each be more important than "adding another attention module." It was exactly this failure that pushed me toward the real problem of my graduation project: do not rush to invent a complex network. First understand why a strong baseline is strong, and then see where there is still room for improvement. Relearning from nnU-Net During the graduation project stage, a senior helped me reproduce nnU-Net. This step was crucial. What makes nnU-Net powerful is not only its network structure, but the way it systematizes a large amount of "engineering experience" in medical image segmentation. It automatically configures preprocessing, patch size, network topology, training strategy, and post-processing according to the properties of the data. So in many cases, it is not just an ordinary baseline, but a very solid segmentation pipeline. The nnU-Net paper also mentions that it can outperform many specially designed methods across multiple public medical segmentation tasks without heavy manual tuning. After reproducing nnU-Net, I finally had a more reliable reference. Then I read work related to FracSegNet. Instead of directly segmenting everything inside the full CT volume, it decomposes the task into two steps: first locating the left hip bone, right hip bone, and sacrum, then segmenting major and minor fragments inside the target bone regions. It also introduces a fracture distance map, or FDM, which makes the model pay more attention to regions near fracture contact surfaces. This idea inspired me a lot. The most troublesome part of fracture segmentation is often not whether the whole bone can be segmented, but whether a tiny gap between neighboring fragments gets filled, whether small fragments are missed, and whether strange false positives appear near broken ends. The overall Dice score may already look very high, but if two bone fragments that should be separated are stuck together by the model, the spatial relationship in 3D reconstruction and preoperative planning becomes completely different. In other words, this task does not need "roughly similar." It needs "the local structure must not be messed up." The New Paper from March Just after I finished reproducing nnU-Net and FracSegNet, while I was still worrying about how to improve further, my advisor gave me a new paper from March. The method was called SCNP, short for Same Class Neighbor Penalization. The starting point of the paper is clever: many segmentation models perform well on the overall region, but cannot guarantee accurate topology. For example, thin structures may break, small regions may appear out of nowhere, and originally separated structures may become stuck together. SCNP does not redesign the network. Instead, during training, it performs neighborhood propagation on logits: foreground positions are affected by weaker responses among same-class neighbors, while background positions are affected by more confusing responses among same-class neighbors. Intuitively, it means the model cannot pass by only predicting the center voxel well. It also needs to care about the most error-prone places among nearby same-class neighbors. This idea immediately matched pelvic fracture segmentation. The problem of fracture fragments is exactly a local structure problem. A narrow gap being filled, a small fragment being swallowed, or a false positive appearing near a broken end are all typical cases where "the large overall region looks fine, but the local connection relationship is wrong." SCNP also has an attractive engineering property: it mainly changes the logits before loss calculation during training. It does not require changing the inference process, nor does it require redesigning an entire complex network. However, directly applying SCNP to pelvic CT also carries risks. CT has noise, and there are stable bone regions far away from fracture surfaces. If neighborhood propagation is applied everywhere, it may amplify local errors in irrelevant regions too. So my graduation project made a compromise: combine the FDM idea from FracSegNet with SCNP, using the fracture distance map as a spatial gate so that SCNP acts more strongly near the high-risk fracture contact surfaces. In one AI-style sentence: do not make the model nervous across the whole bone; make it more serious where things are truly likely to go wrong. What My Graduation Project Actually Did In the end, the core of my graduation project can be summarized into three things. First, I reproduced and organized the baseline pipeline for pelvic fracture CT segmentation. The experiments used nnU-Net as the unified framework, comparing Max-flow, standard nnU-Net, the reproduced FracSegNet baseline, and different SCNP variants. The labels were also reorganized into three semantic classes: background, major fragments, and minor fragments. Second, I introduced SCNP neighborhood structure propagation before loss calculation. It does not change the inference structure of the network. During training, it makes locally difficult regions participate more directly in optimization, thereby complementing the insufficient constraints of CE + Dice on fragment boundaries, small gaps, and local connectivity. Third, I combined FDM and SCNP into a gated version. FDM-gated SCNP concentrates structural propagation near fracture surfaces and reduces unnecessary propagation in stable bone regions or noisy areas. In the experiments, I roughly compared different receptive fields and gating thresholds, and finally found that was a relatively balanced setting. Under unified local post-processing and the same evaluation protocol, FDM-gated SCNP achieved more balanced results compared with the reproduced FracSegNet baseline: All DSC reached , All LDSC reached , All HD95 was , and IoU was . Compared with the FracSegNet baseline, HD95 decreased by about , and IoU improved by about . Of course, these numbers should not be understood as "the problem is solved." There are no such easy victories in medical imaging. They are more like evidence for a small and specific point: on top of a strong baseline, if the training objective is pushed a little toward local structure, the model can indeed become more stable in boundary distance, local Dice, and fragment separation quality. Beyond the Results: What I Really Learned The most useful part of this graduation project was not a certain metric, but the way my understanding of "innovation" changed. At first, I thought innovation meant adding modules, changing structures, and drawing a more complicated network. Later I realized that in a real task, innovation is sometimes the opposite: explaining the problem clearly. Is the whole segmentation inaccurate, or are local boundaries unstable? Is model capacity insufficient, or does the loss function fail to punish the truly important errors? Do we need a larger receptive field, or do we need to constrain the propagation range? My first U-Net did not beat the baseline. That is certainly nothing to brag about, but it forced me to admit that my understanding of the task was too shallow. Later, reproducing nnU-Net and FracSegNet showed me that strong methods are not strong out of nowhere. They consider data organization, label design, training strategy, post-processing, and evaluation metrics together. Finally, introducing SCNP was not because it sounded new, but because it happened to respond to the recurring local structure errors in this task. From the student innovation project to the graduation thesis, this project felt like taking a long detour. At first I wanted to build a system, then I realized the algorithm behind the system was not good enough. I went on to modify the model structure, then discovered that casually adding modules was meaningless. I began reproducing strong baselines, and only then gradually saw the real problem. Finally, I returned to a very small change: during training, let the model look more carefully at the hardest nearby region. Maybe this is what a graduation project is for. It does not necessarily make you build something that changes the world, but it lets you go through a complete learning process with frustration included. You learn how a result comes into being, and you also learn why it is still not good enough. Problems That Are Not Over Yet Of course, this work still has many limitations. The current label space is still a three-class semantic segmentation of background, major fragments, and minor fragments. It cannot truly output an instance ID for every individual fragment. For complex multi-fragment cases, especially very small fragments, unified post-processing may still miss or merge fragments. FDM gating also depends on task priors. The threshold and receptive field mainly come from experimental selection and have not yet become an adaptive mechanism. More importantly, improvement in segmentation metrics does not mean clinical value has been fully validated. If this work continues in the future, the results should be put into downstream tasks such as 3D reconstruction, reduction planning, and surgical path design, to see whether improvements in local boundaries can bring real benefits to the workflow. But at least for me, this graduation project has already completed its most important task: it took me from "can it run?" to "why design it this way?" It also let me truly understand for the first time that the hardest part of an algorithm project is often not writing the network, but finding the errors worth optimizing. items.title: Mac Terminal Setup Notes
items.content_text: For exploration and fun, my old terminal had been stuffed with oh-my-zsh and all kinds of plugins. At some point I could no longer remember what I had installed. Worse, the interface looked so awkward that I did not even want to open it. Recently I saw Ghostty on Bilibili, along with a few terminal customization videos that looked surprisingly nice. So this time I decided to start from zero and rebuild my terminal properly. I started using the terminal shortly after I bought my Mac and finished setting up the development environment. Back then I knew almost nothing about customization tools like Raycast or Bartender, let alone the command line habits that macOS users often build over time. Later, my older cousin tried to teach me a few things. When he opened my computer, he exclaimed: "Why is your computer so primitive?" That was probably the first time I realized how different macOS habits could be from Windows habits. I have always preferred simple setups on Windows too, but from that moment on I started exploring how to make my Mac environment both prettier and more useful. A Messy Beginning For a long time, my terminal looked close to the default style. I forgot to keep screenshots, but it was basically a gray background with plain text. Following different online tutorials, I installed iTerm2, oh-my-zsh, and a large number of other plugins. The problem was that the whole setup became too messy. I either forgot how to use some plugins, or simply never used them at all. The terminal still worked, but it often required plugin updates, and opening a new terminal window had more than a second of delay. That became annoying. So I decided to rebuild everything and write down the process. It may also serve as a reference for classmates who recently bought a Mac and want a clean terminal setup. Sharpen the Tools First Choosing the right tools is the core of this rebuild. My criteria were simple: Performance first: short startup time and fast rendering. Low maintenance cost: usable out of the box, easy to customize, clear configuration path, and not dependent on plugin stacking. Good looking: good looks are productivity. : In the end, I chose this combination: Ghostty + native Zsh + Starship + Yazi. It covers my current needs almost completely, and I can add smaller tools later if needed. After such a long time, I realized I barely used most of the old oh-my-zsh plugins. Installing oh-my-zsh again does not make much sense for me right now. This article also shares a similar idea: A Guide to the Zsh Line Editor with Examples. Let me briefly introduce the tools. Ghostty: Terminal Emulator The official docs describe it like this: Ghostty is a fast, feature-rich, and cross-platform terminal emulator that uses platform-native UI and GPU acceleration. Similar tools include Terminal.app, iTerm2, Warp, WezTerm, Alacritty, Kitty, and more. Why did I choose Ghostty among so many options? I first noticed it because Boris Cherny recommended it. I tried it and unexpectedly found that it fit me very well. It is compiled from Zig to native machine code, avoiding VM/interpreter overhead and GC pauses. Its character buffer maps directly to GPU memory, skipping CPU round trips. It parses TOML configuration once at startup and does not rely on plugin hot reload, which makes it fast. The configuration is also centralized in one TOML file, so settings are clear and easy to understand. After using it for a while, Ghostty starts much faster than my previous setup, and memory usage is reasonable. It feels close to what I imagine a modern terminal should be. For exploration and fun, my old terminal had been stuffed with oh-my-zsh and all kinds of plugins. At some point I could no longer remember what I had installed. Worse, the interface looked so awkward that I did not even want to open it.

Recently I saw Ghostty on Bilibili, along with a few terminal customization videos that looked surprisingly nice. So this time I decided to start from zero and rebuild my terminal properly.

I started using the terminal shortly after I bought my Mac and finished setting up the development environment. Back then I knew almost nothing about customization tools like Raycast or Bartender, let alone the command line habits that macOS users often build over time.

Later, my older cousin tried to teach me a few things. When he opened my computer, he exclaimed: "Why is your computer so primitive?"

That was probably the first time I realized how different macOS habits could be from Windows habits. I have always preferred simple setups on Windows too, but from that moment on I started exploring how to make my Mac environment both prettier and more useful.

A Messy Beginning

For a long time, my terminal looked close to the default style. I forgot to keep screenshots, but it was basically a gray background with plain text. Following different online tutorials, I installed iTerm2, oh-my-zsh, and a large number of other plugins.

The problem was that the whole setup became too messy. I either forgot how to use some plugins, or simply never used them at all. The terminal still worked, but it often required plugin updates, and opening a new terminal window had more than a second of delay. That became annoying.

So I decided to rebuild everything and write down the process. It may also serve as a reference for classmates who recently bought a Mac and want a clean terminal setup.

Sharpen the Tools First

Choosing the right tools is the core of this rebuild. My criteria were simple:

  1. Performance first: short startup time and fast rendering.
  2. Low maintenance cost: usable out of the box, easy to customize, clear configuration path, and not dependent on plugin stacking.
  3. Good looking: good looks are productivity. :)

In the end, I chose this combination: Ghostty + native Zsh + Starship + Yazi. It covers my current needs almost completely, and I can add smaller tools later if needed.

After such a long time, I realized I barely used most of the old oh-my-zsh plugins. Installing oh-my-zsh again does not make much sense for me right now. This article also shares a similar idea: A Guide to the Zsh Line Editor with Examples.

Let me briefly introduce the tools.

Ghostty: Terminal Emulator

The official docs describe it like this:

Ghostty is a fast, feature-rich, and cross-platform terminal emulator that uses platform-native UI and GPU acceleration.

Similar tools include Terminal.app, iTerm2, Warp, WezTerm, Alacritty, Kitty, and more.

Why did I choose Ghostty among so many options? I first noticed it because Boris Cherny recommended it. I tried it and unexpectedly found that it fit me very well.

  • It is compiled from Zig to native machine code, avoiding VM/interpreter overhead and GC pauses.
  • Its character buffer maps directly to GPU memory, skipping CPU round trips.
  • It parses TOML configuration once at startup and does not rely on plugin hot reload, which makes it fast. The configuration is also centralized in one TOML file, so settings are clear and easy to understand.

After using it for a while, Ghostty starts much faster than my previous setup, and memory usage is reasonable. It feels close to what I imagine a modern terminal should be.

Starship: Prompt Engine

Similar tool: oh-my-posh.

Starship is written in Rust and distributed as a compiled program. It starts very quickly. As a prompt engine, it replaces the main use case I previously relied on oh-my-zsh for: making the prompt look nice.

The old setup had to run a pile of shell scripts every time the terminal opened. Now startup is faster, and the whole experience feels much smoother.

Yazi: Async File Manager

Yazi is somewhat like macOS Finder, but controlled through the keyboard. Once you understand your machine's file structure, it feels more efficient than constantly typing cd and ls.

It is also written in Rust, so loading is fast. It supports live previews, which means you do not have to find a file and press Space just to inspect it. It can preview text, images, and many other files directly.

It also uses Vim-style keybindings. If you have used Vim before, it feels natural. Even if you have not, you can probably learn the basics quickly, and the ? help menu is friendly.

Reproducible Setup Steps

Prerequisites

Install Homebrew, the command-line package manager for macOS, and a Nerd Font for terminal icons.

Install Homebrew:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Update Homebrew:

brew update

Install the Software

# Font
brew install --cask font-jetbrains-mono-nerd-font

# Terminal emulator
brew install --cask ghostty

# Prompt engine
brew install starship

# File manager + preview dependencies
brew install yazi ffmpegthumbnailer sevenzip poppler jq fd ripgrep fzf

# Other useful tools
# Command autosuggestions + syntax highlighting
brew install zsh-autosuggestions zsh-syntax-highlighting

Configure Ghostty

Open Ghostty and press Command + ,. A TOML config file should appear. You can copy my config into it:

# ===== Font settings =====
font-family = JetBrainsMono Nerd Font
font-size = 14

# ===== Window padding =====
window-padding-x = 12
window-padding-y = 12

# ===== Cursor and scrolling =====
cursor-style = block
scrollback-limit = 10000
copy-on-select = true

# ===== Theme =====
theme = Catppuccin Mocha

# ===== Quick terminal: Cmd + backtick =====
keybind = cmd+`=toggle_quick_terminal

Next is Starship. You can also read the official Starship configuration docs.

mkdir -p ~/.config && touch ~/.config/starship.toml

items.content_html:
Recently, while wandering around GitHub, I came across a project that felt both shocking and funny: voice-input-src. It is a voice input tool built for Mac.

When you opened the repository, you will not find any traditional Swift source code. Instead, the repo contains only an extremely detailed prompt written for AI, specifically Claude, with both Chinese and English instructions.

That made me curious: Can this kind of open source actually work? Can users really reproduce a usable app from this? Since I happen to have a MacBook, I decided to try reproducing it on my own machine and see whether this open-source model was feasible.

Project Breakdown: Is This Really "Source Code"?

1. An Extremely Minimal Repository

The project has a README.md file containing the required prompt text, and nothing else.

I have to admit, this kind of open-source project is very easy to understand.

2. Prompt as Source Code

Traditional open source is "humans read code, compilers execute code." This project is more like "humans read the prompt, AI executes the prompt."

The author, yetone, even created a separate voice-input-dist repository to store the app source code generated by AI. This cleanly separates the "source" from the "artifact," and it also makes comparison easier for users.

It is a small but interesting design choice.

What Is Hidden Inside the Prompt?

Since the prompt is basically the only thing we can inspect in this repository, I analyzed it before trying to reproduce the project.

This is not a casual requirement document written by someone who knows nothing about programming. It is a document written by someone who clearly understands macOS APIs and implementation details.

Module Implementation Details
Speech Recognition Uses Apple's Speech Recognition framework, supports streaming transcription, defaults to Chinese.
Global Hotkey Listens to the Fn key through global event monitoring with CGEvent tap, while suppressing the default behavior to prevent the emoji panel from opening.
Floating UI Borderless NSPanel, visual blur effects, and real-time waveform animation driven by audio RMS rather than fake animation.
Input Method Compatibility Detects the current input method, switches to the ABC keyboard before pasting to avoid Cmd+V interception, then restores the original input method.
LLM Post-processing Calls an OpenAI-compatible API for correction, only fixing obvious mistakes such as "配森" -> "Python".

From these details, it is clear that the author knew exactly which frameworks to call, which components to use, what conflicts might appear later, and how those conflicts should be handled.

Because the author understands the technical background and implementation difficulties well enough, he could write such a precise project-level prompt. One GitHub issue even commented:

This thing is the real prompt development tutorial.

My Reproduction Attempt on My Mac

To verify whether this kind of open source is actually effective, and also to experience this slightly wild form of prompt engineering, I ran a complete "from prompt to app" experiment on my Mac.

1. Environment

  • Mac: My 2021 M1 Pro MacBook, running Tahoe 26.3.1.
  • AI tool: Codex, using GPT 5.4 Extra High. I wanted to see whether a model different from the author's Claude setup could still succeed.

Here is my device configuration:

2. Steps

  1. Feed the prompt: Send the full prompt from the repository to Codex.
  2. Functional acceptance testing: Definitely not because I do not know Swift well enough to read all the generated code.

Checklist:

✅ Can the Fn key reliably start recording without opening the emoji panel?
✅ Does the floating waveform change in real time with volume?
✅ How accurate is Chinese recognition? Does LLM correction work?

3. Actual Implementation

On my machine, the app did not build successfully on the first attempt. The first full build took about 23 minutes and cost $1.3994 USD. After that, two small runtime/build issues appeared, so I asked Codex to fix them twice. Including fixes, the total cost was $1.9734 USD.

Here is Codex's summary of the two fixes:

These two fixes essentially solved one compile-time problem and one runtime crash.

The first fix was in PasteboardInjector.swift line 18. The original code used an expression like pasteboard.pasteboardItems?.map { ... } ?? [], relying on Swift to infer the type of items. In some cases, this optional chain plus empty-array fallback made type inference unstable, eventually causing an error at return PasteboardBackup(items: items). The fix was simple: explicitly write items as [Item]. This did not change any business logic; it only replaced "let the compiler guess" with "tell the compiler the type directly."

The second fix was in FloatingPanelController.swift line 93. The original code set collectionBehavior = [.canJoinAllSpaces, .fullScreenAuxiliary, .moveToActiveSpace, .ignoresCycle]. The issue is that .canJoinAllSpaces and .moveToActiveSpace conflict semantically. One means "join all Spaces," while the other means "move with the currently active Space." AppKit is sensitive to this kind of window behavior combination, and it can trigger an assertion that ends as an abort signal crash. The fix changed it to a more stable combination: keep .moveToActiveSpace, .fullScreenAuxiliary, and .ignoresCycle, add .transient, and remove .canJoinAllSpaces. The floating window can still appear in the current Space and alongside full-screen apps, but it no longer crashes during initialization.

Result

You can probably guess it: this entire article was dictated using the generated app.

The effect is actually pretty good. Characters appear quickly, faster and more immediate than Apple's built-in dictation, and invoking it is more convenient.

Here is what it looked like:

As for shortcomings, you can see that the text was not centered nicely at first, which felt a bit uncomfortable. I later prompted Codex to fix that too. Overall, my version still did not look as polished as the author's Claude-generated demo, but at least it worked.

Is This the Future of Open Source, or Just a Joke?

1. The Positive View: Extreme DRY

  • Very low maintenance cost: The author does not need to care about Xcode version changes or Swift syntax evolution. He only provides a requirements document.
  • Reproducibility: As long as the AI model is capable enough, anyone can generate a functionally similar app at any time.
  • Easy sharing: This way of sharing is direct. Compared with publishing a huge codebase vibe-coded from scratch, a carefully written prompt may actually be cleaner in some cases.

2. The Slightly Negative View

  • Uncontrollability: Generated code quality depends heavily on the AI model. It is hard to guarantee identical results every time. My Codex version was usable, but visually not as good as the author's demo.
  • Operational friction: To generate the code, users still need an AI environment and enough budget. For small projects this is fine, but larger projects can become expensive. Users also have to wait for generation, which is less convenient than downloading a release from the author.

Overall, I do not think this experiment is a bad thing. On the contrary, the author's creative repo structure gave me a small shock.

Maybe this should be understood less as a concrete project distribution method and more as an excellent AI tutorial. To write a prompt like the author's, you still need solid technical knowledge and a clear understanding of the target platform.

When I look back at the childhood photos my parents took for me, I still feel warm inside. I don't actually remember much from those years, but by watching old videos with my parents time and time again, and hearing them tell those stories time and time again, made even memories that never truly should be existed in my mind become vivid. Maybe that's why many classmates are surprised I can remember things from so long ago. items.content_text: Itinerary: 3/22: Train at 8:50 AM - Arrive in Guangzhou at 12:30 PM - Dim sum at Dian Du De - Chen Clan Ancestral Hall - Liwan Lake - Yongqing Fang - Shangxiajiu - Shamian Island - Canton Customs - Sacred Heart Cathedral - Beijing Road - Guesthouse - Dafo Temple 3/23: Early morning meetup with a new friend at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall - Walk to Nanyue King Museum - Bamboo-pressed noodles - Yuexiu Park - Dongshankou - Taikoo Hui - Gym - Saizeriya - Huacheng Square - Canton Tower - Haixinsha - Guesthouse 3/24: Guangzhou Museum of Art - Sun Yat-sen University - APM Line - Xihua Road - Train station Last Friday, our database teacher took a day off, which unexpectedly gave us free time and turned into a three-day mini holiday. Taking this chance, my close buddy and I planned a trip to Guangzhou, and we also wanted to meet his childhood friend there. So we set off early on Friday morning. My ticket was to Guangzhou East Station. Normally, stations named "East" or "West" are newer and larger. But this one felt the opposite. Guangzhou must have developed so early that even the later-built stations already feel old. The moment we walked out, we were in a bustling district: shiny commercial streets mixed with aging residential blocks, with a few thick, old, lively trees on both sides of the road casting shade over the wide sidewalks. We gradually tuned into the rhythm of the city. It took us a while, but eventually we caught it: long history, rich daily life, youth, and vitality. We quickly decided to go for morning tea. My buddy asked several classmates, and they all recommended Dian Du De. It was a little pricey, but the quality and service were excellent. We went to the branch closest to the station there were a few izakayas across the street; stepping in felt like entering a Japanese drama, totally different from the lively Chinese street outside , and started feasting. The two of us spent 250 RMB and basically tried a whole range of dishes. After the meal we took an elevator, then realized it only went up. Buttons from floors 4 to 11 were all lit and couldn't be canceled. So my friend and I, together with an elderly man, just kept riding floor by floor and eventually came back down to the ground from what had originally been the second floor. The old man chatted in Cantonese, different from what you hear in Hong Kong movies, and complained about a lot of things. I only clearly understood one phrase: "damn it." Just like Lu Xun wrote, that phrase is nationally unified. After that we quickly checked off all the recommended spots from Xiaohongshu. During the process, we slowly resonated with Guangzhou itself: we watched elderly bands playing in riverside parks along the Pearl River, seniors doing partner dancing, little opera stages in parks, filmed with foreign friends, saw young influencers posing at check-in spots, watched young office workers hurrying by, middle-aged people exercising steadily, elementary school kids choosing ice cream after class, parents picking up children after work, and children still playing before their parents arrived. Day one ended quickly. We were exhausted and looked forward to deep sleep that night. Three-Person Walkabout Early on the second day, we skipped refined breakfast shops and went to a roadside stand at a quiet crossroads. We had rice noodles for 5 RMB, and they were surprisingly great 🎉. We met my buddy's childhood friend at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall. At first we were not familiar, just acquainted, and didn't talk much. After visiting the memorial hall together, we passed a Taoist temple on our way to the Nanyue King Museum. Somewhere along that walk, the awkwardness faded and our conversation gradually opened up. After the Nanyue King Museum, we went to a noodle shop that our friend's childhood friend said was good. Unexpectedly, the bamboo-pressed noodles were made with fish-bone broth. I didn't eat a single bite I don't like seafood 😟 , and we continued on. After wandering for a long time, none of us knew what to do next, so I suggested going to the gym our friend's childhood friend is incredibly fit! . We found a cheap gym, but it required reservation and wouldn't let us train on the spot. So we switched to a better one. The service was excellent, and the equipment was new and great. I learned a lot from him. I updated my training plan, clarified my training goals, learned many new movements and details, and also checked whether my existing form was standard. I benefited a lot. Then we went to Canton Tower. Another day ended in complete exhaustion. Train Delay We got up early and walked again to the Guangzhou Museum of Art, because we had forgotten to reserve Guangdong Provincial Museum and couldn't get in. After a quick visit, we arrived at the gate of Sun Yat-sen University. I had already contacted another close friend studying there. He told us about a side gate where we could enter directly without prior reservation since we failed to reserve in advance . He also kindly told us which places on campus were worth visiting. Seeing him study in such a beautiful place made me really envious. I started imagining that one day I could study there too. Then we took a taxi to the APM line, where we heard we could see flowers, but the queue was too long. So we refunded and switched to a snack street. We tried many new foods there. One snack called bo bo gui looked like rice cake with brown sugar syrup, but it turned out to be garlic oil. It left a bad smell in our mouths and was salty, not very tasty. After eating, we rushed to the train station, expecting to arrive on time according to plan, but ran into unexpected traffic and delays. We even cut into line at the station and sprinted all the way to the gate, but were still stopped. If we had arrived just five minutes earlier, we could have made it such a pity . Then came ticket changes. My buddy couldn't get a refund after the train departure and lost 388 RMB. I paid over 110 RMB in service fees to change mine. We didn't get back to Xiamen until 10 PM. Overall, those three days were full and joyful, with rich experiences, both ups and downs. This season is actually a great time to visit Guangzhou. The sun is strong, but it's not unbearably hot. We walked so much that we were completely worn out, averaging 38,000 steps per day. I sincerely hope that one day I can study in Guangzhou, or even stay there for a while and truly live there.

items.title: Notes from Xi'an
items.content_text: AI translation notice: This English version was translated from the original Chinese article with AI assistance. Some nuances may differ from the original. October 27: Wake up at 4:30 a.m. and go to the airport → arrive in Xi'an at 9:50 → first lunch stop Cantonese beef hot pot → Terracotta Warriors Museum → Bell Tower → Muslim Quarter → Drum Tower → Bell Tower → homestay October 28: Wake up at 6:50 a.m. → buy medicine → meet Le-ge → walk on the city wall → Beilin Museum → Shaanxi History Museum → homestay → Giant Wild Goose Pagoda → Great Tang All Day Mall → homestay October 29: Wake up at 7:00 a.m. → Small Wild Goose Pagoda → airport An Exciting Day — October 27 Our flight left at 6:50 in the morning, so I needed to get up around 4:30 and go to bed early. I lay down at 11:30 but did not fall asleep until around one. All night I kept thinking that the next morning I would finally feel the autumn air of a place that felt like home. I was incredibly excited. When it was time to get up, I was surprisingly not tired at all. I set off for Xi'an full of energy. After arriving in Xi'an, we took the metro and followed our plan toward the Terracotta Warriors. We stopped to eat along the way because a restaurant's flyer looked interesting. The food was fine, but coming all the way to Xi'an to eat Cantonese food made the Guangdong member of our group feel personally defeated. Xi'an is very good at tourism. The metro stations had notes explaining which public-transport route to take to famous attractions, as well as how much a taxi should cost and how long it should take. This helps prevent visitors from being overcharged by unscrupulous drivers. I was genuinely moved by the effort this city had made to think about its visitors. We then reached the Terracotta Warriors . There was a little disappointment: two of the three people in our group decided not to hire a guide, so we went without one. After quickly walking through the three pits, we ran out of time and missed the Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang. We also did not make it to Huaqing Palace, which is supposedly not that impressive anyway. Dinner that night was quite good. The restaurant was neither famous nor conspicuous, but according to the owner of the osmanthus-cake shop, it was authentic. When we asked for “Lao Liu's Lamb Paomo,” the shopkeeper's eyes lit up as she happily explained how to get there. Perhaps it really was good. The Wind on the City Wall — October 28 I woke up with irritated eyes because the homestay was not very clean, so I activated the Sharingan first thing in the morning. I went out to buy medicine and wasted more than ¥80. From now on, I will always bring some common medicines when traveling. After meeting Le-ge, we bought an egg-stuffed flatbread from a street stall. Eating a simple, ordinary, piping-hot breakfast in the slightly chilly autumn air felt like a small piece of human happiness. It was even more satisfying than eating a full meal in the warm cafeteria at my university in Xiamen. There were not many people on the northern section of the city wall, so we rode bicycles. The air was not very humid and felt much lighter, almost as though I did not need to inhale because it would flow into my lungs by itself and fill me up. My body seemed lighter too, as if buoyed by water. From the wall, the entire layout of Xi'an unfolded in the distance. The feeling of having one's expectations fulfilled was wonderful. The autumn wind refreshed me and blew away my stress; for a young person, perhaps this wind could not yet carry melancholy. Watching the kindergarten children running a “marathon” along the wall made the whole scene feel even more energetic. The Shaanxi History Museum was also completely without a guide. It was crowded, the space was relatively small, and the stuffy air made it difficult to settle down and appreciate the exhibits. The artifacts were all national treasures, and the guides seemed professional, but after one pass I did not retain a particularly deep impression. It was hard not to compare the museum with those I had visited before, especially since it is already such a remarkable institution. It might be more exciting if museums could exchange artifacts with other countries, allowing visitors to see the histories of different regions from the same period side by side. The British Museum offers something like that. As for the building itself, it is also hard to compare with the National Museum of China: one is narrow and crowded, the other grand and spacious. Despite these shortcomings, the Shaanxi History Museum left a strong impression on me. I hope I can return someday and listen to a proper guided tour. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda and the Great Tang All Day Mall at night were genuinely awe-inspiring. The street design showed a lot of thought and encouraged visitors to interact with it: piano-key paving stones, dance-floor-style tiles that changed color, and fountains whose flow was controlled by the sound of the crowd. There were many performances along the street, including a viral “Mimou” show and a concert. The street was broad enough that even with imposing historical sculptures in the middle, snack stalls on both sides, and girls in Tang-style clothing taking photos along the edges, everyone could still walk around freely. The buildings along the street were thoughtfully designed as well. The books displayed in the Xinhua Bookstore's reading room were niche without being bizarre, numerous without feeling disorderly, and ornate without being gaudy. Someone was playing the piano, and the space was perfect for one person to calm down after the bustle outside and read without interruption. The books also suited Xi'an as a city. A bookstore really can be a city's soul. The Osmanthus Rice Ferment drink from Chahua Nong that night was genuinely delicious. When I had something similar from Chabaidao on October 30, the flavor was nowhere near as impressive. Chahua Nong emphasized the rice ferment and tea, while Chabaidao pursued the sweetness of osmanthus so single-mindedly that it lost the flower's clean fragrance. The Journey Home — October 29 We woke up a little late today and everyone slept comfortably. My body, however, had begun to react to the change of season, and my nose felt terrible. We only took a quick look at the Small Wild Goose Pagoda from the entrance because we were out of time, then continued to the airport. We did not talk much on the way. We were savoring this spontaneous, slightly fantastical journey as we boarded the plane back to Xiamen. It felt as though I had gained a little more sense of belonging to Xiamen. I still had more than two years left there, but I wondered when I would truly feel that I was also a part of the city.

The air was not very humid and felt much lighter, almost as though I did not need to inhale because it would flow into my lungs by itself and fill me up. My body seemed lighter too, as if buoyed by water. From the wall, the entire layout of Xi'an unfolded in the distance. The feeling of having one's expectations fulfilled was wonderful. The autumn wind refreshed me and blew away my stress; for a young person, perhaps this wind could not yet carry melancholy. Watching the kindergarten children running a “marathon” along the wall made the whole scene feel even more energetic.

The Shaanxi History Museum was also completely without a guide. It was crowded, the space was relatively small, and the stuffy air made it difficult to settle down and appreciate the exhibits. The artifacts were all national treasures, and the guides seemed professional, but after one pass I did not retain a particularly deep impression.

It was hard not to compare the museum with those I had visited before, especially since it is already such a remarkable institution. It might be more exciting if museums could exchange artifacts with other countries, allowing visitors to see the histories of different regions from the same period side by side. The British Museum offers something like that. As for the building itself, it is also hard to compare with the National Museum of China: one is narrow and crowded, the other grand and spacious.

Despite these shortcomings, the Shaanxi History Museum left a strong impression on me. I hope I can return someday and listen to a proper guided tour.

The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda and the Great Tang All Day Mall at night were genuinely awe-inspiring. The street design showed a lot of thought and encouraged visitors to interact with it: piano-key paving stones, dance-floor-style tiles that changed color, and fountains whose flow was controlled by the sound of the crowd. There were many performances along the street, including a viral “Mimou” show and a concert. The street was broad enough that even with imposing historical sculptures in the middle, snack stalls on both sides, and girls in Tang-style clothing taking photos along the edges, everyone could still walk around freely.

The buildings along the street were thoughtfully designed as well. The books displayed in the Xinhua Bookstore's reading room were niche without being bizarre, numerous without feeling disorderly, and ornate without being gaudy. Someone was playing the piano, and the space was perfect for one person to calm down after the bustle outside and read without interruption. The books also suited Xi'an as a city. A bookstore really can be a city's soul.

The Osmanthus Rice Ferment drink from Chahua Nong that night was genuinely delicious. When I had something similar from Chabaidao on October 30, the flavor was nowhere near as impressive. Chahua Nong emphasized the rice ferment and tea, while Chabaidao pursued the sweetness of osmanthus so single-mindedly that it lost the flower's clean fragrance.

The Journey Home — October 29

We woke up a little late today and everyone slept comfortably. My body, however, had begun to react to the change of season, and my nose felt terrible.

We only took a quick look at the Small Wild Goose Pagoda from the entrance because we were out of time, then continued to the airport. We did not talk much on the way. We were savoring this spontaneous, slightly fantastical journey as we boarded the plane back to Xiamen. It felt as though I had gained a little more sense of belonging to Xiamen. I still had more than two years left there, but I wondered when I would truly feel that I was also a part of the city.

I arrived in Chaozhou at night. I waited a long time for K2, then spent another hour on the bus. It took real effort to reach my destination. During that time I made a video call to my family, basically "livestreaming" while walking to my guesthouse. Without that call, I would have felt much more tired. Honestly, it saved me a lot of energy. The rental was a bit expensive, but worth it. With it, I zipped through Chaozhou Ancient City Archway Street and also visited the market area. It gave me a much deeper understanding of Chaozhou. The archways on Archway Street commemorate all kinds of outstanding successful exam candidates. I felt I understood history a bit more deeply at least that no matter what official position, once you passed the imperial exam, it was enough to erect an archway and be remembered by later generations . Guangji Gate, Guangji Bridge. Only after walking the entire bridge did I understand the origin of "Guangji": it was built through donations from wealthy people and institutions at home and abroad. Because I got up early, I became the first person to step onto Guangji Bridge that day, and the first to reach the broken-bridge section. Watching how the floating bridge connects was truly interesting. No wonder it's known as one of China's four great ancient bridges. I visited many places that day. The biggest disappointment was Thai Buddha Temple and Huiru Park. They face each other across a road, both in poor maintenance condition. Around them were many aggressive touts trying to squeeze out the last bit of value, which made it hard on many tourists who followed online guides. If I had to choose one unforgettable memory today, aside from the sights, it would be a photo I didn't take I was tasting herbal tea then, and it was really hard to drink ☹️ . The photo should have been a quote on the steps at the entrance of Hanwengong Ancestral Hall: Diligence perfects skills, play wastes them; action succeeds through thought, and fails through conformity. The five words "perfect," "waste," "play," "fail," and "conform" kept me thinking. I couldn't help admiring Han Yu's precise wording. No wonder he is considered the foremost of the Eight Great Masters of Tang and Song. Even though I didn't take that photo, I pretended to read the line once before leaving, then kept thinking about it all the way. Isn't that line describing me? Especially the word "play": it's not simply the opposite of diligence, like laziness or indecision, but indulgence. When someone is busy indulging, it's hard to realize one's own faults. "Half the soldiers die before the battle, while beauties still sing and dance in the tents." "Warm winds intoxicate travelers, and they mistake Hangzhou for Bianzhou." Ruined by conformity — "Those who think by following public opinion are people who block their own ears and eyes." This immediately reminded me of Nietzsche. I keep reminding myself to seek perspectives from different angles. But following public opinion is just too easy, and it spreads responsibility so thin that no one seems accountable. Even if you're wrong, you may not be mocked, and you often bear no real consequence. The hardest part is that you may not even notice you've been trapped by it. 9.24 If you don't use time well, how can you know how precious it is? When I got to Shantou, I was honestly overwhelmed by what I had seen the night before. I stayed in Shantou's commercial center, and there were crowds everywhere. I wandered MixC again and saw all kinds of people and many shops I'd never seen before. What struck me most was seeing some elementary-school-aged kids walking around the mall without parents when I was their age, I was only riding a bike around my neighborhood . They casually took out their phones, shot photos, posted content, spoke in internet memes, and little girls copied influencer makeup and photo poses in front of escalators. It made me feel just how different this era is. I became really curious about what their childhood will feel like when they look back in the future. All these scenes made me think the city was very developed. In the morning I went to the hospital my eye got inexplicably inflamed the day before and swelled badly . Seeing a familiar hospital environment calmed me down. Last night had been too dark to see clearly, and the lights had dazzled me. This trip made me use time fully. If I had stayed in my dorm that weekend, I probably would have just browsed the web, complained a little, and studied inefficiently. But this time, during waiting-for-registration time alone two and a half hours , I visited an entire museum, walked through an entire park, and tried guozhi for the first time. It had been a long time since time felt this slow or maybe this full . In the past, this amount of time would have been just waking up, eating, and staring at a computer. Only when you truly use each slice of time well do you realize how rich and precious time is. Traveling Alone In the past, traveling alone was something I didn't dare do. Online, people also try to explain how lonely they are with examples: watching a movie alone, eating hotpot alone, going to the hospital alone, traveling alone. After this trip, I had done all of those. Loneliness is still hard to avoid. Whether at scenic spots or restaurants, seeing couples, groups of friends, and happy families naturally stirs envy. Luckily, WeChat sharing helped. I shared my travel photos and videos with my parents. When someone is there to share with, even a boring trip still carries meaning. Freedom is the biggest feature of traveling alone. If my eye hurts, I go to the hospital without worrying about delaying anyone, and I get to see what local hospitals are like . I don't need to consider other people's appetite or thoughts. Once I decide, I just do it. That saves a lot of energy, since the only person I need to convince is myself. So my pace became much faster. I went wherever I wanted. If I got bored, I moved on; if not, I stayed and daydreamed. And without someone beside me to constantly joke and complain with, my mind became more focused. It was no longer noisy group playfulness that makes you miss details. I had more time to observe my surroundings and try to understand them. It felt like a more mature state of mind.
